Many airlines, hotels, theme parks and cruise lines pay year-round tribute to military service members with generous discounts and benefits. Sometimes these deals are available only to active-duty military personnel, and at other times the perks extend to U.S. military veterans and their families.

Related: The best credit cards for active-duty military members: Get waived annual fees

No matter the form these military travel deals take, they all reflect the gratitude the travel industry feels toward those who have sacrificed so much to protect our country.

Here are the perks that military members can take advantage of on their travels in 2026.

To honor military members, B Hotels & Resorts offers an exclusive “B Saluted” discount of 15% off regular rates for military members, veterans and their families. Florida-based B Hotels & Resorts has locations in Fort Lauderdale and Marathon.

Through the "Honoring Our Heroes" program, Sandals and Beaches resorts in Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Antigua, the Bahamas, Grenada, Barbados, Curacao, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines offer a 10% discount to eligible U.S. military members and veterans.

Best Western properties across the U.S. offer discounted rates for veterans, military members and government personnel.

Best Western’s Service Rewards program — the hotel chain’s free award program tailored to military and armed forces members — unlocks even more member benefits, including an automatic upgrade to Gold status and bonus points on qualified stays.

In November, military members can receive 10% off their stay at Big Cedar Lodge, as well as 25% off resort activities including a spa day pass, golf simulators, bowling and more.

Through the Waves4Warriors Club, CheapCaribbean Vacations offers active-duty service members, veterans and military families access to exclusive deals, room upgrades, special perks and savings of $150 off a qualifying five-night or longer vacation package after you join at hotel brands including Breathless, Dreams, Zoetry, Royalton and more.

Choice Hotels — including Comfort, Sleep Inn and Quality Inn hotels — offers discounted rates for official and leisure travel to active-duty and retired military personnel, their dependents and members of several military associations. When you are searching for a hotel, open the drop-down "Rate" menu and choose "Military/Veterans (Leisure)" for leisure travel or "Government/Military (Official Business Travel)" for work travel.

Active-duty military members, veterans and military spouses are eligible to join the Choice Privileges rewards program at the Gold Elite level.

Extended Stay America offers discounted rates to military members at three brands and more than 650 locations across the U.S. To receive the discount, choose "Government & Military" from the dropdown box during booking.

Great Wolf Lodge offers up to 40% off nightly rates for active, retired and veteran military members through the Howling Heroes offer. The offer is valid for up to two guests per room, with a $20 fee per additional guest.

The Grove Resort & Water Park is a one-stop hotel and water park only a short drive from Walt Disney World. Military members can receive up to 20% off the best available rate when booking through this link.

Federal and U.S. military employees qualify for military rates and discounts at participating Hilton properties. There are separate discounts for official and leisure military travel. For official military travel, check the box labeled “Government and military rates” to apply the rates. For leisure travel, visit Hilton's Military Family Rate page and search for your travel destination and dates.

Veterans, active-duty members and their immediate family members are eligible for a discount of 10%-15% off Hyatt’s standard rate at participating U.S. hotels. To get the discount, use the offer code "MILVET" while booking.

The hotel chain behind brands such as InterContinental, Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza and Kimpton offers a military rate at participating locations worldwide. The rate applies to active-duty military personnel, veterans, retired military personnel and their families.

Margaritaville Beach Resort's "Salute to Heroes" rate offers up to a 35% discount to active-duty service members and veterans.

Marriott Bonvoy offers discounted federal, state and local government rates available to government and military personnel. To access the discounted rates, choose the “Government & Military” option from the “Special Rates” drop-down menu when searching for a stay. You’ll get a list of all the Marriott Bonvoy properties in your chosen city that offer special rates and their eligibility requirements.

Motel 6, along with its sister extended-stay brand Studio 6, offers a 10% discount on standard rates to active and retired military personnel.

Active-duty military personnel, veterans and government employees are eligible for a 10% discount on official travel at any U.S. Red Roof location. The hotel chain also has a 10% discount on leisure travel for all government employees and military members, veterans and retirees.

If you are traveling to Hawaii for military business or leisure, The Surfjack offers a range of military discounts. With the "Get Shacked @ The Jack" promotion, military members can save 25% on room rates, bring a pet for free and receive discounts on dining and parking.

TradeWinds Resort in St. Pete Beach, Florida, offers up to 25% off its best available rates to military members when you use code "Military" at booking.

Participating Wyndham properties offer discounts of up to 15% off their best available rate to active and retired military personnel, veterans and their families. Plus, qualifying military personnel and their spouses get automatic Gold status when they enroll in the Wyndham Rewards program and bonus Wyndham Rewards points for qualified stays.

In some markets, Alaska Airlines offers discounted military fares to active-duty military personnel and their dependents when you call 800-252-7522 to purchase your tickets. The airline also offers discounts through the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel can board early, check up to five bags for free, receive 15% off inflight food purchases and receive complimentary day passes to visit an Alaska Lounge when traveling on official government-sponsored travel. All other active-duty military personnel can purchase a discounted lounge day pass for $40.

U.S. active-duty and reserve military members, military veterans, members of the National Guard and their dependents get up to two pieces of checked baggage for free through the Allegiant Honors program. Also, the airline waives its typical fees for oversized checked baggage, a carry-on bag, getting a boarding pass printed at the airport, bringing a pet on board, seat assignments and change or cancellation fees due to a change in orders or directives. Qualifying service members can also board their flights early.

American Airlines offers government or military fares in some markets, but you must call the airline at 800-433-7300 to book. Veterans and their families can access reduced fares by enrolling in the WeSalute+ program.

Active-duty military personnel are also allowed Group 1 boarding privileges, and they can bring up to five free checked bags when traveling on orders and up to three free checked bags when traveling for leisure (weight restrictions apply).

U.S. military personnel traveling in uniform on a same-day American flight can enter Admirals Club lounges with their immediate family — defined as a spouse, domestic partner and/or children under 18 — or up to two guests at most Admirals Club locations except for Airspace Lounge at San Diego International Airport (SAN) and Japan Airlines' Sakura Lounge at Honolulu’s Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL).

Active-duty U.S. service members can call Delta Reservations at 800-221-1212 for discounted fares unavailable to the general public. Delta also offers priority boarding and free checked baggage to active-duty military members. The number of bags you are allowed depends on the type of travel and fare type, and you must adhere to the specified baggage size and weight restrictions.

Frontier typically charges for carry-on bags and checked baggage. However, active-duty armed forces, National Guard and Reserve members, their accompanying spouse and children can receive a free carry-on bag, two free checked bags and one free personal item.

Active-duty military personnel traveling for business or leisure are eligible for a 5% discount on base fares. If traveling on government-sponsored business, call 800-538-2583 to receive your discount and up to five free checked bags (military members traveling for leisure get up to two free checked bags). This discount applies to you and your immediate family.

U.S. active-duty military members, retired military members, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families enrolled in WeSalute+ can also get a 5% discount on base fares and up to two free checked bags.

Special fares are available for military and government travelers, but you must call the airline at 800-435-9792 or visit the airport ticket counter to book them. Additionally, military members traveling on active duty receive priority boarding before Group 1 and are exempt from the two-piece baggage limit.

United offers an additional checked baggage allowance, priority boarding and United Club lounge access to active-duty military members traveling in uniform. U.S. military veterans, active-duty military members, National Guard and Reserve members, and their families are also eligible for a 5% discount on United-operated flights.

Active-duty U.S. military personnel, spouses and dependents are eligible for a 10% discount on the lowest available fare in select fare classes. Select “Military” for each eligible passenger during your ticket search on Fare Finder. Amtrak also welcomes uniformed military personnel to the front of the ticket line.

All U.S. SeaWorld, Busch Gardens, Aquatica and Sesame Place parks offer discounted tickets to active-duty military members and veterans through the Waves of Honor program. Most parks also offer at least one complimentary admission per year.

Disneyland honors active and retired U.S. military personnel with discounted one-, three- and four-day Disney Military Promotional tickets. The three- and four-day tickets include access to Disneyland and Disney California Adventure each day of your ticket, while the one-day ticket is good for entry to one park only (excluding blackout dates). Pricing starts at $98, and you must purchase tickets at a participating U.S. military base ticket office or through govx.com. Theme park reservations are required.

Hotel discounts are also available by calling 866-309-9737.

Dollywood offers discounted tickets and annual passes to U.S. active or retired military members, veterans, military reservists, spouses and dependents.

Military members who visit the home of America's first president can save $4 on admission tickets, while Purple Heart recipients and active-duty members in uniform receive free admission all year long. Every year on Veterans Day, however, all active-duty, former or retired military personnel receive free admission and can participate in an annual tribute by placing a flower on General Washington's tomb.

Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, offers discounted daily tickets and season passes to active, retired and veteran military members. To access this discount, purchase online or present your government ID at the park's ticket booth.

Most U.S.-based Merlin Entertainments attractions offer discounted military tickets, but a handful of locations are giving away free tickets to military members and veterans through Nov. 30. These include Legoland parks in Florida and New York, Madame Tussauds Orlando and Sea Life Aquariums in Orlando, Grapevine, Texas, Kansas City, Missouri, and San Antonio, Texas.

Active duty and retired military personnel and veterans, along with their spouses and dependents, can purchase a Military Passport season pass starting at $119.99.Silver Dollar City also offers a ticket discount to U.S. active or retired military personnel, veterans and military reservists, along with their spouses and dependent children (ages 4-17) living in their households.

In addition to discounted tickets, Silver Dollar City invites all military members and veterans to help raise the American flag during the park’s daily opening ceremony. Service members are also given a red, white and blue ribbon to wear in the park, allowing employees and guests to thank them for their service.

St. Augustine has hundreds of years of military history, much of which you can still visit today. The city shows its appreciation to military service members year-round with discounts on accommodations, attractions and experiences.

Universal Orlando offers a Military Freedom Pass promotional ticket to all active-duty and retired service members. Ticket prices start at $220 for unlimited admission between now and Dec.18, 2026, though blackout dates apply. Each eligible service member can purchase up to six promotional tickets and must buy them through a participating authorized military ticket and travel office. Military members can also purchase discounted tickets to the new Universal Epic Universe park.

Universal Studios Hollywood offers discounted tickets to active-duty, retired and eligible veteran military members, along with their spouses and dependents. Additional on-base discounts are available, including a 12-month Military Pass.

Active and retired U.S. military personnel are eligible for discounted hotel rates and specially priced theme park tickets at Walt Disney World. Military members can purchase a Military Salute ticket with either Park Hopper or Park Hopper Plus starting at $409 for a four-day ticket, $429 for a five-day ticket and $449 for a six-day ticket. Disney World also offers a special ticket valid for multiple visits through Dec. 18, 2026, starting at $499.

Blackout dates apply, and theme park reservations are required. Hotel stays can be booked by calling 407-939-7830. Tickets must be purchased at a participating U.S. military base ticket office to avoid being charged a sales tax, but are also available at Disney World ticket windows.

Vail Resorts offers Epic Military Passes for active-duty service members, retired military members and veterans. Prices start at just $230 for unlimited skiing at more than 40 Vail Resorts and discounts on family passes, food, lodging, gear rentals and more.

AmaWaterways offers active and retired service members a special military discount of $250 per person off a river cruise or enjoy two-for-one cruise fares on select 2026 and 2027 sailings when you use the code "MIL250" or "MIL2FOR1" when booking.

Carnival Cruise Line shows its appreciation for active and retired members of the armed forces with discounted cruise rates, onboard credits and reduced deposits. Additionally, some ships have a Heroes Tribute Lounge, and every ship holds a military appreciation gathering for service members and their families.

On select Celebrity Cruises sailings, active and retired military members can save $25 on inside and ocean-view cabins and $100 on veranda cabins and above, and these savings can be combined with other current promotions. This discount applies to the first and second guests in the cabin.

Disney Cruise Line offers special rates to all military members, active and retired, and their spouses. Discounted rates are only available on select sailings. To honor America's 250th anniversary, the cruise line is offering a $250 onboard credit for eligible U.S. military personnel on select Disney Wish and Disney Dream sailings in 2026.

MSC Cruises offers discounted fares to all active and retired U.S. military personnel, as well as family members traveling with them. You can receive a discount of 5% on interior and ocean-view cabins, 10% on balcony and suite cabins, and a “kids sail free” promotion on select sailings.

Margaritaville at Sea honors active and veteran military members with a free cruise through the Heroes Sail Free program. On select sailings, military members and an additional guest in the same cabin can get a free fare (taxes and fees are not included). A third and fourth guest can be added at the regular fare. On all other sailings, military members can save 20% off the retail fare for the first four guests in the cabin.

Norwegian Cruise Line’s Military Appreciation program extends exclusive benefits to military members, veterans and their spouses. Members of the program receive up to a 20% discount on select sailings.

Veterans and active, retired and disabled military personnel can receive up to $250 free onboard spending money on select Princess Cruises sailings. You can use this onboard credit for specialty dining, onboard boutiques, shore excursions, spa treatments and more.

Royal Caribbean offers military rates to active and retired personnel, veterans and their spouses. The discounted rates also apply to friends and family members staying in the same cabin as the eligible service member. The best way to access the discounted rate is to book through a travel agent or to book directly with Royal Caribbean over the phone.

A host of benefits awaits travelers who have served or are serving in the U.S. military.

Because these military travel deals, their requirements, and the eligibility of family members, spouses and dependents vary, carefully research each military discount offer to avoid surprises. Many airlines, hotels and other businesses might ask for proof of eligibility, so don’t leave home without the military ID, veteran ID, dependent ID, orders and/or other documentation you’ll need to take advantage of the many travel offers.

#6182. Highest To Lowest: How To Get From JFK To Manhattan For Just $3

In the film Highest 2 Lowest (2025), starring Denzel Washington, legendary filmmaker Spike Lee portrays two distinct sides of New York City, depending on your altitude and bank account. Nowhere is that contrast more apparent than in the choices travelers face when commuting between Manhattan and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Whether you are a visiting traveler or an NYC resident, navigating to and from the city’s primary international hub is a perpetual balancing act between cost, comfort, and time. Previously, I detailed what is literally and figuratively the “highest” mode of airport transit: Blade’s helicopter transfers (starting at $195 and easily topping $300, though rides can cost you nothing out of pocket using Bilt Cash). Each Bilt Cash award expires 12 months after you earn it, on the last day of that month.

In this Reader Story, I’m taking you down, subterranean, to the lowest option available: the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) $3 bus-to-subway hack.

Duke Ellington was onto something: “Take the ‘A’ Train.” However, he didn’t specify which A train branch, nor did he mention that a quick bus transfer might be involved!

Even some locals may ask: “Wait, isn’t the AirTrain $8.75, plus a $3 subway fare?” That’s true if you exit the AirTrain at Jamaica or Howard Beach. However, there is a lesser-known and dramatically cheaper workaround: just $3 total from JFK to nearly anywhere in NYC with the MTA, provided you don’t mind adding a few extra minutes to your journey.

For the reverse trip, take any Lefferts Blvd-bound A train, ensuring the destination sign explicitly says “Lefferts Blvd” rather than Far Rockaway or Rockaway Park. Importantly, Far Rockaway A trains often display “JFK Airport” on their digital side displays because most travelers use the more expensive $8.75 Howard Beach transfer route, so do not board those if you want the $3-only route. Once on the correct train, get off at Liberty Ave / Lefferts Blvd, exit to the street, locate the bus stop, catch a JFK-bound Q10 or Q80 bus to the Lefferts AirTrain station, and take the free AirTrain directly to your terminal.

If you type “JFK Airport” into Google Maps or Apple Maps, the app will almost never display the $3-only hack. Navigation algorithms prioritize minimizing the number of transit transfers over saving money, automatically suppressing the bus transfer in favor of the standard $8.75 AirTrain connection at Jamaica or Howard Beach.

Even typing “Lefferts Blvd AirTrain Station” into navigation apps often causes confusion because the AirTrain station and the Ozone Park A-train terminal are located roughly 1.5 miles apart.

To force your map app to show the correct route, search for the street-level bus-to-subway transfer point at “Lefferts Blvd & Liberty Ave.” From JFK, this will display the Q10 Rush or Q80 bus taking you to the A train turnstiles; from Manhattan, it will guide you on the Lefferts-bound A train directly to your bus connection.

Other than extreme weather events, strikes, and major crises, all three legs of this route—the AirTrain, the Q10/Q80 bus, and the A Train—operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, though timing varies. During daytime and peak hours (6:00 AM – 10:00 PM), AirTrain cars run every 7–10 minutes, Q10 and Q80 buses depart roughly every 8–15 minutes, and A trains run frequently as express services through Brooklyn and Manhattan.

However, late-night transit frequency changes significantly in NYC, so keep that in mind for overnight or early-morning flights: AirTrain headways drop to 15–20 minute intervals, late-night Q10/Q80 bus departures stretch to every 20–30 minutes, and the A train may shift to local-only service (check MTA Service Status for possible re-routings).

Thanks to the flat-fare structure of the New York City Subway (as opposed to distance-based transit networks found in cities like London, Tokyo, or Washington, D.C.), that single $3 fare (and free transfer) unlocks access to nearly the entire city once you pass through the turnstiles at the Ozone Park–Lefferts Boulevard station.

Because there are no exit turnstiles or zone caps inside the subway network, you can ride from Queens through Brooklyn, up Manhattan, and deep into the Bronx, all on that same initial $3 tap—as long as you stay within the fare-paid zone. And, if you exit the subway system in Lower Manhattan, you can walk over to Whitehall Terminal and board the free Staten Island Ferry to reach the fifth and final borough. While attempting to tap onto a Staten Island bus or the Staten Island Railway (SIR) on the other side would consume a second $3 fare (and likely break the 2-hour transfer clock), at least JFK to Manhattan for $3 remains one of the greatest transit bargains in the world.

All told—AirTrain, bus, and subway—you can get between JFK and Manhattan in about 75 to 90 minutes. Depending on brutal rush-hour highway traffic, you might even tie or beat a $100+ rideshare. That said, I would recommend this route exclusively for those traveling light (backpacks and carry-ons), willing to spend the extra time, and comfortable navigating city transit. But for the right traveler, it is a relatively safe, clean, reliable, and wildly affordable hack.

To put the $3 bus-to-subway hack into perspective, it helps to see how it stacks up against the other primary options for traveling between Manhattan and JFK:

Of course, there are other, less conventional ways of getting to and from JFK:

Whether taking a $300+ helicopter ride or a $3 bus-to-subway hack, commuting between JFK and Manhattan truly captures the two contrasting sides of New York City that Spike Lee brings to life in Highest 2 Lowest.

For light packers on a budget, the Lefferts Boulevard Q10 transfer stands as the undefeated champion of pure value. Duke Ellington was right all along—if you want to get to Sugar Hill or anywhere else in the city without breaking the bank, simply take the “A” train!

With so many options available, what’s your preferred way of getting to or from JFK, and which are your preferred payment methods to maximize value?

#6181. Southwest Airlines Launches 5 New International Routes: See Full List Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Southwest Airlines will launch a total of five new international routes to its growing network, as the world's largest operator of the Boeing 737 debuts a number of new services during the Northern Hemisphere winter season.

The newest route, which took flight on November 1, connects Las Vegas to Mexico, while more routes are expected to come online at the beginning of 2027. This article will examine Southwest's five new international routes during the winter travel season, which runs from October 25 through March 27, 2027.

Dallas-based Southwest's newest international route connects Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) to Mexico's Pacific Coast, with up to six weekly flights to Puerto Vallarta (PVR). The route, which began on November 1, becomes the airline's third international service from the Nevada airport after Cancun International Airport (CUN) and San Jose del Cabo (SJD).

For travelers to Puerto Vallarta, Southwest operates year-round to Denver (DEN), Houston (HOU), Las Vegas (LAS), Orange County (SNA), Phoenix (PHX), St. Louis (STL), and San Diego (SAN). Seasonal destinations include Austin (AUS) and Sacramento (SMF).

Southwest is Puerto Vallarta's second-largest international carrier by total destinations served, with nine. This follows Canadian carrier WestJet with 12, and ahead of both United and Delta at six.

Beginning in the New Year, Southwest continues to expand from Nashville, as the hybrid airline begins a new nonstop service to both Liberia (LIR) in Costa Rica and a link to the picturesque island of Aruba (AUA).

These services will be uncontested, with Southwest being the only airline connecting to the two cities nonstop. Southwest remains the biggest airline at Nashville by far, with more than 56% of all market share at the airport. This is ahead of both American Airlines and Delta.

Southwest operates up to 60 nonstop routes from Nashville to key destinations across the United States. It has a handful of international routes including Cancun and San Juan (SJU) year-round, while expanded seasonal destinations include Aruba (AUA), Montego Bay, Jamaica (MBJ), San José, Costa Rica (SJO), Cabo San Lucas, Mexico (SJD), and St. Thomas, US Virgin Islands (STT).

Southwest maps international expansion with nonstop links from Nashville and Austin to popular resort destinations.

The final two international routes launching this winter include the airline's latest service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to San Jose (SJO). The direct link to the capital of Costa Rica starts on March 13. Southwest remains the largest airline at Austin, maintaining around 41% of all commercial flights, ahead of Delta, which is aggressively expanding at the Texas airport.

From Austin, Southwest operates to 45 destinations nonstop, with existing international routes including Cancun and San Jose del Cabo. Upcoming international routes in the winter will include San Jose, while more additional routes will kick off later next year to Nassau, Punta Cana, and Liberia.

Columbus (CMH) will gain an additional nonstop international route this March, with Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic becoming the airline's newest route. The service will compete head-to-head with Breeze Airways. Other winter international routes from Columbus with Southwest include Cancun, San Juan, and Punta Cana.

#6180. Lufthansa Takes Delivery of Its First A350-1000

Lufthansa this week took delivery of its first Airbus A350-1000, a type it says will offer a better customer experience while reducing operating costs.

The aircraft was formally handed over to the carrier on Tuesday in the presence of Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr and Lars Wagner, CEO of commercial aircraft at Airbus. Nicknamed “Deutschland,” the jet is Lufthansa’s 700th Airbus airplane, and the seventh in a special commemorative fleet bearing 100th anniversary liveries.

The white and dark blue designs feature an oversized crane, a symbol first used by predecessor Deutsche Luft Hansa.

Lufthansa Group has ordered a total of 15 A350-1000s. The first 10 will operate for the Lufthansa core brand, and will be based at its Munich hub.

“Deutschland” will fly to Munich on Wednesday, officials said, and operate its inaugural flight, to Tokyo-Haneda, on Dec. 3. The aircraft will also be Lufthansa’s first long-haul airplane equipped with Starlink satellite internet service.

“The fact that, as the world’s largest Airbus customer, we are taking delivery of our 700th Airbus aircraft exactly 50 years after the first Airbus delivery to Lufthansa, and in the year of our 100th anniversary, makes this a very special moment for us,” Spohr said in a statement. “Our partnership is a prime example of what Europe can achieve when it works together.”

Lufthansa’s -1000s will seat 300 passengers in four cabins – First, Business, Premium Economy, and Economy.

When it comes to earning credit card rewards, sometimes two cards really are better than one.

Maybe you have a card that earns bonus points on dining and groceries but falls short on other everyday purchases. Or perhaps you love your card's travel perks but wish it offered better earning rates outside of travel.

That's where pairing cards can come in handy. By choosing two cards with complementary benefits and earning categories, you can get more out of your spending without relying on a single card for everything.

Here are three American Express card combinations worth considering, depending on your spending habits and travel goals.

Frequent travelers who want a combination of premium travel benefits and strong everyday earning rates may get the most value from pairing the with the .

The Platinum is, at its core, a travel and lifestyle card that offers access to an extensive network of airport lounges worldwide through the Global Lounge Collection, along with a range of statement credits and other travel benefits.

The Gold fills an important gap in the Platinum's earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $50,000 and $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, respectively*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

By using the Platinum for eligible flights and the Gold for dining and groceries, you can earn elevated rewards across several major spending categories while enjoying premium travel benefits. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can also combine your rewards into one balance to use toward travel through Amex's transfer partners (after linking your accounts online).

The trade-off of this card combination is cost. The Platinum has an $895 annual fee, while the Gold has a $325 annual fee, bringing the combined annual cost to $1,220. For that reason, I'd only recommend this pairing to travelers who can take advantage of the Platinum's benefits and who regularly spend in the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: How these two cards got me over $4,500 in value in one year

If you spend a lot on dining and groceries but want to earn more than 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases, the and could make a great pair.

The Gold earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year*) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year*). It also earns 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

Then, use the Blue Business Plus for eligible business purchases that would earn only 1 point per dollar on the Gold. It earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*) compared with the Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up a single rewards balance to use toward travel through Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Gold has a $325 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee, so you won't pay extra to add a flat-rate earning card to the mix.

Just keep in mind that the Blue Business Plus is a business card, so you'll need to qualify to apply. This combination could be especially useful for freelancers and small-business owners with eligible business expenses that don't fall into the Gold's bonus categories.

Related: The 4 Amex cards I’d use to earn Membership Rewards points faster

If your business spends a lot on things like advertising, software or gas, the and could make a great pair.

The Business Gold earns 4 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in combined purchases per calendar year*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

What I like about the Business Gold is that you don't have to choose your bonus categories in advance. Amex automatically determines your top two eligible categories each billing cycle, which is helpful if your business expenses change from month to month.

For purchases outside those categories, the Blue Business Plus earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*). That's double the Business Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

For example, you might use the Business Gold for advertising and software expenses, then switch to the Blue Business Plus for other eligible business purchases. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up one balance to use with Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Business Gold has a $375 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee. This combination makes the most sense if you spend enough in the Business Gold's bonus categories to justify the annual fee while using the Blue Business Plus to earn more on other purchases.

Related: 7 reasons why the Amex Blue Business Plus Card should be in everyone’s wallet

Before adding another Amex card to your wallet, take a look at where you're spending the most money and what you want to get out of your rewards. The goal is to find a card that fills a gap in your current lineup, rather than one that offers more of the same.

And remember, earning more points isn't worth it if you're spending more than you normally would or carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: Best credit card strategies for couples

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to choosing the best credit card combination. The key is finding cards that complement each other rather than simply offer more of the same benefits.

Whether you're looking for premium travel perks, stronger everyday earning rates or a way to maximize rewards on business expenses, pairing the right Amex cards can help you earn more Membership Rewards points.

Just make sure the additional rewards and benefits are worth the combined annual fees and that you're choosing cards that make sense for your spending habits.

#6176. Which Airlines Are Dry (No Alcohol)? Can You Bring Your Own Alcohol?

For many people, alcohol is an aspect of traveling by air that they enjoy. I’m not just talking about first or business class travel, where a glass of champagne might be part of the fun. Airports are also one of the few places where you can have a drink at 5AM and not be judged (too hard).

Admittedly customs differ around the globe, based on culture, religion, etc. In this post, I thought it would be interesting to talk a bit about dry airlines, as there’s a bit of nuance to this.

Which airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard? Which airlines don’t serve alcohol but let you bring your own alcohol? And does all of this even matter?

Let’s start by taking a look at the airlines that are dry, meaning that they don’t serve you alcohol. Here are the airlines that come to mind:

Admittedly that list isn’t totally exhaustive, since there are a countless number of small airlines out there. However, I think this covers the biggest and most interesting airlines that don’t serve alcohol (though if I missed any major ones, please let me know).

There’s an interesting twist to this. While some airlines are dry, they’ll let you bring your own alcohol onboard, and then you can consume it (within reason). The following three international carriers come to mind:

Now, it’s important to note that this isn’t without strings attached:

When I flew Kuwait Airways several years back, I wrote about how we brought a bottle of wine onboard, and they gladly let us consume it. It’s not that I couldn’t be without alcohol, but I was curious to experience a BYOB concept on a plane, since that was novel for me.

There’s an added layer of complexity to all of this, as there are some airlines that aren’t generally dry, but are dry on certain routes. Several situations come to mind (let me know if I’m missing any):

As you can tell, in some of the above situations, the lack of alcohol presumably has little to do with religion or concerns over behavior, and more to do with controlling costs.

People have different takes as to how “bad” it is to fly on a dry airline. On the one end of the spectrum, there are people who will avoid dry airlines at all costs. On the other end of the spectrum, you have billions of people who don’t drink alcohol at all, so this is a non-issue.

Personally I’m probably somewhere in the middle:

Regarding that last point, I do have to give credit to airlines that are dry, but still put effort into their drink selection. Take Saudia, for example, which goes above and beyond in terms of its non-alcoholic drink selection in premium cabins, with everything from cappuccinos and espressos, to excellent mocktails, to non-alcoholic wine.

Airlines often reflect their local customs and religions, so it’s not surprising that many airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard. If you definitely want alcohol when you fly, avoid airlines like Saudia. If you would like a drink when you fly, the good news is that some dry airlines actually let you bring your own alcohol, within certain limitations.

While the above doesn’t cover 100% of situations, hopefully it’s a useful, basic rundown of some of the bigger airlines that are dry.

How strongly do you feel about dry airlines? Does this policy impact your airline choice?

#6174. Flight Attendant Finds Hidden Camera In Lavatory—Passenger Charged With Trying To Erase Evidence

A flight attendant found a hidden camera in a Scoot lavatory. The passenger onboard the Singapore Airlines low cost carrier accused of putting it there is also charged with deleting evidence. It’s the deleting that creates the greatest risk of imprisonment. The incident happened October 7 on Scoot flight TR821 from Osaka to Singapore. The 52-year-old British passenger was charged in Singapore on November 5. One Mile at a Time flags the story noting he’s currently jailed. He’s now been offered S$10,000 bail. The man plans to plead guilty. According to the Singapore Police Force, the man concealed a camera in a lavatory, left, and activated recording through an app on his phone. A female flight attendant discovered the device while using the lavatory. She removed it and alerted a colleague. Police say Lutley later tried to retrieve it, found it missing, and deleted the app and related photographs to avoid detection. Officers detained him when the flight arrived at Changi Airport and seized both his phone and the camera. That’s some fancy police work! The Alleged Deletion Carries The Biggest Penalty He faces one count each of: Voyeurism: up to two years in prison, with a fine also available. Obstructing the course of justice: up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both, over the alleged deletion of the app and photographs. While the voyeurism law includes caning, Singapore exempts men over 50 so he’s in the clear there. The United Airlines Passenger Who Recorded Himself In 2019, I wrote about a United Airlines passenger accused of hiding a camera in the first class lavatory on a San Diego – Houston flight. A woman found the device and handed it to a flight attendant. The camera had recorded the man installing it. Investigators matched his clothing and jewelry to airport footage. They also recovered deleted files showing women in an Emirates lavatory, including a flight attendant. And there’s the American Airlines case where a family alleged the airline gave a flight attendant time to erase evidence after a teenage passenger discovered his phone attached to a toilet seat with maintenance stickers. Federal prosecutors later confirmed that the crewmember had reset his phone, while investigators found recordings of other children in his cloud account. He received an 18 1/2 year prison sentence last year. (HT: One Mile at a Time) Topics on this pageHidden cameraObstruction of justiceScootVoyeurismAmerican AirlinesEmiratesHoustonOsakaSan DiegoSingaporeSingapore AirlinesSingapore Changi AirportUnited Airlines+9 more More From View from the Wing

#6173. Why United Airlines Accepts A 222-Seat Jet Over A Standard 257-Seat One On Its CES Tokyo Route

In January 2027, United Airlines will begin new nonstop flights between Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT) and Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS). This is an unusual launch on the surface, since LAS is not a major hub for the airline, but it is a limited service scheduled around the annual Consumer Electronics Show (CES), held from January 6 to January 9. The carrier will run three NRT-LAS flights on January 3, 4, and 5, and three LAS-NRT nonstop flights on January 9, 10, and 11.

The three NRT-LAS flights before the 2027 CES will use United's Boeing 777-200ER, featuring 276 seats and 50 Polaris seats. The three flights to Tokyo, however, will use the Boeing 787-9 rather than the 777. More interestingly, the airline will use its new Elevated 787-9 with its latest interiors and a premium-heavy configuration, featuring 64 Polaris suites and just 222 seats in total. It's unusual to use two different aircraft on the same route in opposite directions, especially when one has 54 more seats than the other.

While LAS is a large spoke for United, it's not a particularly high-priority market, and the CES services exist to better serve existing Star Alliance customers who need to travel from Asia to CES nonstop, helping retain customer loyalty. In addition, these services also help expand United's and All Nippon Airways' (the two operate a metal-neutral transpacific joint venture) potential customer base, as some customers may have booked away from the two in the past for CES due to the lack of a nonstop.

These routes work because of the sudden surge in demand to Las Vegas during this period, but they won't operate for a long period of time, which means United needs to find extra aircraft capable of operating the route. The 777 is coming from San Francisco, with United scheduling a second daily flight from San Francisco to NRT under the flight number UA 936 on January 2, 3, and 4. In NRT, the 777 turns around for UA 937 to LAS; after arrival, it operates a service to San Francisco again.

The return leg with the 787-9 works slightly differently. United has not scheduled a domestic leg to LAS with the Elevated 787-9, which means that the aircraft will need to be ferried. It then operates UA 7 to NRT, turns around, then operates UA 6 to IAH. Crucially, UA 7 is ordinarily used for the airline's outbound service from IAH to NRT, but this flight simply won't operate on the three days when the LAS-NRT flights are running. In contrast, United is adding a second 777 flight from SFO to NRT to position the aircraft for the NRT-LAS flight.

With these services, United is essentially using spare aircraft capacity, with the 777-200ER fleet having enough slack during those three days to operate a SFO-NRT-LAS-SFO rotation. Meanwhile, the airline felt that it was lucrative to cancel the outbound IAH-NRT leg for three days and use the Elevated 787-9 from LAS to NRT. Importantly, these decisions are being made based on what aircraft is available, not necessarily because the carrier needs to fly the 777-200ER or Elevated 787-9 on this service.

Every business decision comes with an opportunity cost. In the case of the LAS-NRT flight, United chose to cancel the IAH-NRT flight for three days and use that aircraft to operate the LAS-NRT flight, a decision weighed against pulling an aircraft from elsewhere. This doesn't necessarily mean that the IAH-NRT flight is particularly weak, but the math favored this solution above all others. In addition, the Elevated 787-9 could also be particularly desirable for this route.

The Elevated Interior and 222-seat layout debuted only in 2026, while January 2027 will be the first time United operates CES services. Primarily, these flights are about increasing customer loyalty and expanding the customer base, so United is putting its latest and greatest aircraft on this route. The Elevated 787-9 not only has the airline's newest seats, but it also has an extremely premium-heavy layout, and exposing these customers to the best United can offer further supports its mission.

Decisions like these involve multiple factors, including the IAH-NRT flight's performance on the selected days, the value of flying the Elevated 787-9 on LAS-NRT, the opportunity cost of pulling an aircraft from another route, and availability. It's also worth noting that mid-January generally has low travel demand in the US, which may explain why United could source a spare 777 and why United may have been inclined to cancel the IAH-NRT flight for three days. Of course, the airline has not confirmed these reasons.

Delta One and United Polaris are leading business class products, but which one is the better choice? Is network coverage better than luxury?

The Elevated 787-9 has significantly fewer seats than United's standard 787-9, but it has substantially more premium capacity. For the customer base booking flights for CES, the added Polaris and Premium Plus capacity is exactly what is desired, which means that yields will likely remain high while most of the seats will still be filled. As such, the carrier should earn a substantial amount of revenue from operating this route with the Elevated 787-9, even if economy capacity is low.

Although the Elevated 787-9 has significantly more premium seats than the Boeing 777-200ER, the 777 is still a very premium-heavy aircraft. With 50 Polaris seats and 24 Premium Plus seats, the 777-200ER has more premium capacity than the standard 787-9, and it is one of the most premium-heavy aircraft in United's fleet. The use of the 777-200ER demonstrates that the airline clearly saw strong premium demand, even if the return flight uses an even more premium-heavy aircraft.

Offering the Elevated 787-9 on this route may have been United's priority, but the aircraft may not have been available to pull from another service in both directions. This could be why the airline instead pulled a 777-200ER for the flights to LAS, but then took an Elevated 787-9 from the Houston route on days when demand may have been weaker. Because of the limited nature of this route, opportunity cost plays a much bigger factor.

United currently has 51 internationally configured 777-200ERs, while only 16 of its 64 787-9s are in the 222-seat layout with the Elevated Interior. There is a significant mismatch in capacity between the two segments, while premium capacity is actually much higher on the 787. United installs 50 Polaris seats, 24 Premium Plus seats, 46 Economy Plus seats, and 156 standard economy seats on the 777-200ER. Meanwhile, the Elevated 787-9 is equipped with 64 Polaris Suites, 35 Premium Plus seats, 39 Economy Plus seats, and just 84 economy seats.

Inside, the Elevated 787s feature the next generation of Polaris business class seats. Based on the Elevate Ascent, these seats are configured in a reverse-herringbone layout while featuring sliding doors. The screens are larger than the prior generation of Polaris seats, and the airline has configured half of the center seats in a herringbone pattern, creating honeymoon suites that can also partially convert into a double bed. Furthermore, these planes feature front-row 'Polaris Studio' suites.

United's new premium-heavy layout on its Boeing 787-9 fleet is designed to compete with the world's best airlines.

American Airlines has long operated January-only transpacific services from Las Vegas for CES. In 2027, the airline will operate nonstop flights from LAS to NRT and Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN), using a 273-seat 777-200ER on both flights in both directions. As with United's CES flights, American's service will operate only for a limited time, although it is significantly larger than United in this market.

While American is the more established player on CES routes from Asia, Delta Air Lines is growing quickly. In 2027, the carrier will run nonstop flights between LAS and ICN, Hong Kong International Airport (HKG), Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG), and Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE). In addition, Delta is running nonstop flights to London Heathrow Airport (LHR), competing against American Airlines on this route, while also operating flights to Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) and Amsterdam Schiphol Airport (AMS).

These services are all limited, although United is undoubtedly the small newcomer to this market. Overall, this is a small but lucrative market that US airlines are increasingly interested in, but only for a very short period.

#6171. Amex Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 175K Points Welcome Offer (Check Yours)

The American Express Platinum Card® is one of the most popular premium cards on the market, and it currently has an incredible welcome offer that’s as high as 175,000 bonus points, making it the ideal time to apply. In this post, I’d like to go over all the details of the current Amex Platinum bonus, including who is eligible, and why you might want to apply.

While the Amex Platinum has a steep annual fee, it also has compelling perks that will make it worthwhile for many, ranging from lounge access to credits. If you’re eligible for the current bonus, then picking up the card and giving it a try is a no brainer, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

The Amex Platinum Card welcome offer is potentially very lucrative, with a twist. The Amex Platinum bonus is marketed as being as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $12,000 within the first six months. However, Amex notes how the welcome offers vary, and applicants may not be eligible for that welcome offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the Amex Platinum welcome offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer, though I appreciate that Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means I value 175,000 points at a staggering $2,975, making it among the best welcome offers out there. Of course that assumes you’re eligible for this Amex Platinum bonus, which not everyone will be.

The spending requirement is significant, though you do have six months to complete it, so averaging $2,000 per month in spending might not be that hard for many people. There are lots of creative ways to reach minimum spending requirements, including things like paying quarterly taxes by credit card, if eligible.

This is potentially one of the best welcome offers that we’ve ever seen on the card, and publicly available welcome offers don’t get much better than this. In some cases people may be targeted for even bigger offers, but it’s rare. To maximize your odds of getting a targeted offer, make sure you’re opted in to getting marketing communications (by email and mail) from Amex.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to roughly 20 airline and hotel partners, and those are the best ways to get outsized value. These partners range from Air France-KLM Flying Blue, to Emirates Skywards, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer. Just to give a couple of Amex redemption examples:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Platinum Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). The primary reason you’ll want to get the card is because of the extensive perks that it offers, ranging from airport lounge access, to elite status, to credits.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

As you can see, the focus here is almost entirely on credits, lounge access, etc. When it comes to actual return on spending, the Amex Platinum isn’t very rewarding, with limited exceptions:

So this is my go-to card for airfare spending, but other than that, this isn’t a card I spend much on.

Read a full review of the Amex Platinum Card here.

The Amex Platinum Card welcome offer is huge, and is as high as 175,000 bonus points upon completing minimum spending. The structure of this offer is a little unusual, since the offer is “as high as” that amount, and when you fill out your application, you’ll see exactly what offer you’re eligible for (without an impact on your credit score).

If you are eligible for such a big welcome offer, this card is absolutely worth picking up. It offers all kinds of great perks that can help offset the annual fee, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status, and more. Who’s ready for first class on United Airlines’s smallest regional jet?

The first Mitsubishi CRJ-450, a premium variant of the CRJ-200, is “on track” to begin carrying passengers by the end of the year. That's according to Andrew Nocella, United's chief commercial officer, who discussed the arrival of the CRJ-450 on the sidelines of the  brand-new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Monday.

The plane will debut at the airline’s Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) hub, he added.

First look: United unveils gorgeous new Washington Dulles concourse, massive lounge

“It’ll be very exciting and it’s really critical that we connect big cities to little cities, and that’s what the CRJ-450 allows us to do,” said Nocella.

Nocella did not say where the CRJ-450 could fly from ORD but it is widely expected to serve some of the smallest cities in United's network, for example Akron-Canton, Ohio, or Fort Wayne, Indiana.

United unveiled the CRJ-450 in March in an effort to expand its premium offerings to smaller markets. Instead of the usual 50 economy seats on the CRJ-200, the 450 has seven first-class, 16 extra-legroom economy and 18 economy seats — for a total of 41 — a luggage closet for carry ons and high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi.

United's new CRJ-450: Could this be the fanciest regional jet in America?

The CRJ-450 is essentially a premium overhaul to the standard CRJ-200 that has been a workhorse of regional flying for much of this centutry. Passengers have routinely disliked the CRJ-200 for being small and cramped, an experience United hopes to improve with the less-dense CRJ-450 variant.

The plane is similar to the CRJ-550, a 50-seat premium variant of the CRJ-700 that typcially seats around 70 passengers. United debuted the CRJ-550 in 2019.

The CRJ-450 is the smallest plane in United’s premium airplane menu. Larger offerings include the Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” for premium domestic routes, the A321XLR for long-haul routes and up to the Boeing 787-9s with the “elevated” interior that features the new Polaris Studio in business class.

“We have realized that the demand for premium was much higher than we ever knew,” United CEO Scott Kirby, said in March. “It’s like we’re finally creating supply to meet the demand for premium.”

United regional affiliate SkyWest Airlines will operate the first 40 CRJ-450s under the United Express brand. The first two CRJ-200s are undergoing the necessary modifications and certification at one of the Utah-based regional carrier’s maintenance facilities, SkyWest President Wade Steel said at the end of October.

“The first airplanes just take longer naturally just because you’re working through the first-time issues,” he explained. Subsequent CRJ-200 conversions will take 2 to 3 weeks.

Steel, and SkyWest CEO Chip Childs, emphasized that the first CRJ-450s would enter service with United by the end of the year despite at the time having only about eight weeks left in 2026.

Both executives were bullish on the opportunity for the CRJ-450. Steel estimated demand for around 100 aircraft in the coming years as major airlines seek to increase premium offerings across their fleets.

“Putting first class seats on a CRJ-200 in a very good LOPA [Layout of Passenger Accommodation] with an outstanding interior is a very valuable aircraft,” said Steel

Delta Air Lines, for example, joined United in offering the CRJ-550 on regional routes in 2024. SkyWest flies the CRJ-550 for Delta.

American Airlines is the only major U.S. carrier not offering the CRJ-550. However, the airline can fly more larger regional jets, particularly the Embraer E175, than either Delta or United under a more lenient contract with its pilots.

#6168. Military Member Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” Over Denied Free Upgrade

A military member and social media influencer has taken to Instagram to complain about a recent interaction with an Alaska Airlines employee, where he asked for a free upgrade, and was denied. He’s accusing an employee at the airline of being anti-military. Is that a fair complaint, or is this being blown out of proportion?

A military member posted a 2min35sec video online, outlining his experience with an Alaska Airlines representative at Portland International Airport (PDX), which he claims was his first time encountering an “anti-military” employee at the airline. To summarize his version of events:

You can see the video for yourself below. As you’d expect, this guy’s followers are mostly military related, so the 1,300+ comments on the post are almost entirely in agreement with the person who posted the video.

First let me say that I of course respect and appreciate the service of those who are in the military (even if I fundamentally disagree with the extent to which we get into conflicts that accomplish nothing — that’s the fault of our elected leaders, and not the fault of those who put their lives on the line).

Of course if the Alaska Airlines employee in question was rude, that’s not acceptable, and people expect polite service. Now, I’m a little skeptical of how much of a direct transcript this was, rather than how this guy chose to interpret it. That includes things like him suggesting that the Alaska employee accused him of lying. If that were the case, that’s unacceptable, but again, it’s not clear if that was actually said, or just how he was made to feel.

All that being said, this guy sort of strikes me as being rather entitled. Airlines are extremely generous with active duty military members, as they should be. The airline has a page that outlines military and veteran benefits, and upgrades isn’t among those perks. The airline offers all kinds of other things, ranging from special fares, to lounge access, to priority boarding. But it seems a little greedy to then be like “oh, they do all these things, but they should do more” (since he chooses to reference this page).

But here’s my bigger issue with this guy’s approach. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking for an upgrade, but be ready to be shot down. However, I feel like his approach is more one of entitlement than “it can’t hurt to ask.” Why do I say that?

The very example he gives is that for all these times he flies Alaska, either they say “sure, we’ll upgrade you,” or they say “sorry, it’s full, we can’t upgrade you.” In other words, he assumes he’s entitled to the upgrade as long as there are open seats, which just isn’t the policy. If he’s going to be rejected for something he’s not entitled to, he wants to be lied to, rather than told “sorry, that’s not our policy.”

And again, he emphasizes how he has no level of entitlement, but also then argues by pointing out that he has been upgraded for free in the past. It all sounds to me a little like being caught with a liquid that’s too large at the TSA checkpoint, and then trying to argue with them, and say “well last time they let me through.” Well, that’s fine, but that’s not the policy.

So my take here is that airline employees should of course always be professional. I think it’s perfectly fine to say “I’m sorry, that’s not our policy,” which is something this guy seems to take issue with. If the employee did actually accuse him of lying about being upgraded in the past, that’s of course not acceptable. But I’m also not convinced that actually happened.

A military member has accused an Alaska Airlines employee of being anti-military, after being denied a free upgrade to a seat with more legroom. He argues that there’s no harm in asking, but also seems to think that the only acceptable rejection is a claim that the cabin is full.

While Alaska offers lots of perks to military members (as they should), upgrades isn’t among them. Asking once is one thing, but I do find it a bit entitled to essentially believe that you’re entitled to the seats as long as they’re empty, and then to argue if you’re not upgraded.

What do you make of this “anti-military” Alaska employee?

#6167. United’s 1st Private-Jet-Like CRJ450 Set For December Debut In Chicago

United Airlines is preparing to introduce its first CRJ450 regional jets in December, with the aircraft expected to begin operating from Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and Denver International Airport (DEN) before the end of 2026, according to reporting from The Points Guy. The new configuration gives the 50-seat Bombardier CRJ200 a more premium cabin, including a dedicated first-class section, while retaining the smaller aircraft’s ability to serve markets that cannot support larger regional jets. The first aircraft, registered N973SW, was converted from a CRJ200 and is operated by SkyWest Airlines for United Express. Aviation Week confirmed that the first two conversions were still underway in early November.

The launch is part of United’s effort to improve service on shorter regional routes without relying exclusively on larger aircraft. Rather than introducing a new airframe, the CRJ450 repurposes an existing jet with a revised cabin, expanded luggage storage, and onboard Wi-Fi. That approach could give smaller communities access to a more comfortable United Express product, although the airline has not announced a complete list of destinations. Lafayette, Indiana, is one example of a smaller market that could be relevant to the aircraft’s role, but it should not be treated as a confirmed CRJ450 destination.

The CRJ450 retains the CRJ200 airframe but reduces passenger capacity from 50 to 41 seats. Its cabin includes 7 United First seats, 16 Economy Plus seats, and 18 standard economy seats. The reconfiguration creates a two-class product on an aircraft that previously operated with an all-economy layout.

United is also changing how passengers store their carry-on luggage. Overhead bins have been removed from the first-class cabin and replaced with a dedicated closet, giving passengers more open space around their seats. In economy, redesigned overhead bins are large enough to accommodate standard rollaboard bags, addressing a familiar inconvenience on smaller regional jets where larger carry-ons often have to be tagged and placed in the aircraft’s cargo hold.

The aircraft will also feature Starlink Wi-Fi, available free to MileagePlus members, according to United’s March 2026 announcement. However, the CRJ450 will not include the self-service snack bar found on United’s larger CRJ550. The result is a more upscale regional cabin, not a miniature version of a mainline aircraft.

The first CRJ450, N973SW, began life as a CRJ200 delivered in June 2004. Aircraft records from Planespotters list its conversion in March 2026, following its previous configuration as a 50-seat regional jet. United publicly unveiled the concept that same month, but completing the first aircraft has taken longer than subsequent conversions are expected to require.

SkyWest President and Chief Operating Officer Wade Steel told investors during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that the first two aircraft were still being converted. The work includes coordinating service bulletins with manufacturer support partners, with later modifications expected to take approximately two to three weeks per aircraft. Most of the work is being performed at SkyWest’s Tucson, Arizona, maintenance base.

The program is expected to expand substantially after the initial aircraft enter service. SkyWest anticipates converting approximately 50 CRJ200s into CRJ450s by 2028 and has a multi-year agreement with United to operate 40. The regional carrier also sees potential to retrofit additional aircraft used in its own prorate operations, with the broader opportunity potentially reaching 100 conversions. These figures describe different parts of SkyWest’s plans, rather than a confirmed United fleet commitment for 100 aircraft.

United’s 56-seat-economy 767 shows how far the airline is pushing premium.

United says the CRJ450 will primarily connect smaller cities with its hubs in Chicago and Denver. The aircraft’s reduced seating capacity gives the airline another way to offer first-class service in markets where demand may not justify a larger regional jet. It also provides more flexibility under the scope restrictions governing the number and size of regional aircraft that major US airlines can operate through their partners.

Lafayette, Indiana, could be an interesting example of the type of community that might benefit. Purdue University’s home airport has historically relied on limited regional service, and a smaller aircraft could make premium seating available on routes that would be difficult to support with a larger jet. However, United has not identified Lafayette as a planned destination, and the aircraft’s eventual assignments will depend on the airline’s network and commercial decisions. The CRJ450 also follows the strategy behind United’s CRJ550, which uses a modified CRJ700 airframe with fewer seats and a more premium cabin. The newer -450 applies a similar concept to the smaller CRJ200. For SkyWest, converting existing aircraft offers a way to extend the usefulness of its regional fleet while giving United another option for serving smaller markets.

The first aircraft’s December debut will therefore mark more than a cabin refresh. It will test whether United can make older 50-seat regional jets more commercially attractive by selling a better onboard experience, even with fewer seats available. If the initial conversions perform as intended, the CRJ450 could become a more common sight on United Express routes connecting smaller communities with Chicago and Denver over the next two years.

#6165. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6163. Alaska Airlines Launches Global Concierge—Its Answer To United Global Services And American ConciergeKey

Alaska Airlines has started inviting customers into Atmos Global Concierge, its new unpublished invitation-only top tier status along the lines of United Global Services, American Airlines ConciergeKey and Delta 360. The first reports point to an effort to win expensive international business class tickets, with benefits that include a next-flight guarantee during travel disruptions, dedicated assistance and Avis Chairman’s Club. Some of the early reaction has been that the benefits look underwhelming. I disagree. I used to have Avis Chairman’s Club, and it was special. And American’s next-flight guarantee came through for me when I needed it, having this benefit at Alaska could be really clutch. Invitations started surfacing November 9. One recipient shared this language: As one of our most valued status holders, you’ve been selected for two exceptional privileges: a complimentary upgrade to Atmos Titanium status and an inaugural membership in Atmos Global Concierge, our most elevated level of service. The invitation emphasizes travel across Europe, Asia and Oceania, backed by a dedicated team. Global Concierge membership begins immediately and runs through December 31, 2027. You’re invited to ATMOS GLOBAL CONCIERGE by u/iZoooom in AlaskaAirlines Alaska is giving these customers Titanium status and Global Concierge membership. What Atmos Global Concierge Members Get An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion. Direct access to a concierge team. Proactive itinerary monitoring. A next-flight guarantee. Arrival assistance at destinations in Asia, Europe and Oceania. A car transfer at London Heathrow for tight connections. Upgrade priority on global flights. CLEAR+ membership. Avis Chairman’s Club. Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full.
