An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion.

Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier.

There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. #6162. Frontier Airlines’ Unique First Class Now On Sale (No Food, Drinks, Or Recline)

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale, with the product launching systemwide for flights as of March 2027. This is a major development for the Denver-based airline, as the historically ultra low cost carrier tries to move upmarket, and respond to consumer preferences. This is only one of several initiatives we’re seeing, along with the introduction of Starlink Wi-Fi, plus charging ports at select seats. Let’s cover all the details.

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027. For context, Frontier plans to reconfigure its entire fleet to add eight first class seats at the front of the cabin, with two rows of seats in a 2-2 configuration. Specifically, the airline has selected the Geven Comoda seating platform, with seats having up to 37″ of pitch.

Frontier has already started reconfiguring planes with first class cabins, and the idea is that by early March 2027, the entire fleet will have these seats, which is the point at which they’ll be sold as a separate product. So while the seats will already be in service, and some customers will luck out, that’s the formal launch plan.

Obviously this is a fast timeline for retrofitting cabins, but keep in mind most of the cabin will remain unchanged, so it shouldn’t take much time to reconfigure each aircraft. So, what should we expect in terms of the first class product? Here’s how the airline describes it:

First Class seats offer our most spacious seating experience, providing exceptional comfort and additional personal space at the front of the aircraft. These seats are pre-reclined and do not convert into lie-flat beds.

Complimentary food and beverages are not included with the First Class experience. However, a variety of food and beverage options are available for purchase by all passengers.

Frontier’s first class seats will be “pre-reclined” (meaning they won’t recline), and won’t actually offer complimentary snacks and drinks, so it’ll be just like economy in that regard. On the plus side, the seats are expected to feature USB-C charging ports, which will be the first time that the airline offers in-seat power. The carrier is also going from offering no Wi-Fi, to offering Starlink Wi-Fi as of mid-2027, so that’s pretty exciting.

The airline will also be introducing a dedicated extra legroom section in rows three through eight, with seats having up to 34″ of pitch. Not only that, but these seats will also have USB-C charging ports (while the remainder of economy seats won’t offer in-seat power).

With Frontier Airlines first class tickets now on sale, what is pricing like? The airline is increasingly leaning into the concept of bundles, so we’ll see the Basic Fare, Economy Bundle, Premium Bundle, and First Bundle.

The First Bundle includes a carry-on bag and personal item, two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds each, priority boarding, and no change or cancel fees.

Pulling up a random one-way flight from Denver (DEN) to Los Angeles (LAX), I see the Basic Fare starting at $119, the Economy Bundle starting at $142, the Premium Bundle starting at $172, and the First Bundle starting at $244.

Those are some incredibly attractive prices, especially if you intend to check bags. However, the airline emphasizes how it has promotional pricing at launch, so only time will tell how that pricing evolves.

There’s no single right or wrong way to offer a premium product. However, I feel like Frontier might be taking the wrong strategy here. What Frontier is offering is essentially more along the lines of the initial Spirit “Big Front Seat” — you get more space, and nothing else.

This just strikes me as a missed opportunity, because I feel like psychologically, willingness to pay is going to be substantially higher if you just include free alcoholic drinks and at least some sort of food. It’s not like I was expecting them to install ovens and have hot meals (JetBlue’s new first class will only have cold food).

But I feel like if the airline just invested $10 in drinks & snacks they could charge more, and would also expand the potential customer base. Whether logical or not, there are some number of passengers who would be more likely to even consider a product if it actually had a dedicated soft product, rather than just being a more spacious seat. At least that’s my take.

Obviously at the current pricing, this is an incredibly attractive proposition for customers. However, I also feel like the airline probably wants to be able to charge higher fares in the long run.

Frontier Airlines has started to reconfigure planes with first class seats, with tickets now being on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027 (at which point the entire fleet should be reconfigured). While Frontier first class will have first class-style seats (minus the recline), there won’t be any differentiation in terms of the soft product, as food and drinks will still be available for purchase.

I would’ve liked the airline to actually roll out a differentiated soft product, but it sounds like that’s not happening. Then again, between Starlink Wi-Fi and in-seat power, this will be a much more attractive proposition than flying with Frontier in the past.

What do you make of Frontier’s first class concept?

Flew F9 RT TPA LAS and NEVER EVER again. And yes, they could have tossed in at least one comp beverage and snack. Yes, missed opportunity for those good folks that would chose F9. I have fond memories of the original FL and THAT was a great airline.

Honestly, this is exactly the kind of “First Class” Americans deserve. 😂 The same crowd that endlessly whines about European Business Class because “OMG, it’s the same seat as Economy!” — conveniently ignoring the guaranteed empty middle seat, lounge access (yes, even on domestic flights), and generally far superior food and service — now gets a First Class product with a non-reclining seat and not even a complimentary drink. Apparently, the only thing that matters is THE SEAT. Never mind the overall experience. Every nation gets the First Class product — and, apparently, the presidents — it deserves. 🤷‍♂️

I really don't see the problem here. It's smarter to be able to actually be able to deliver the experience that's expected, rather than throwing on food that's going to suck anyway. And while people do certainly like to recline, in shorter hops, it's not all too often I see people reclining all that much in first. Should they throw in a snack or some beverages at least? Yeah, probably. At least Southwest and JetBlue have a good reputation for onboard service and can deliver a little bit of a premium experience. Frontier is not in that list. This is for the Frontier regulars who may actually be well off, but don't see much value in a premium airport/airplane experience. You're still in a metal tube and all of the limitations thereof. Or others that want to splurge, when it may still be less than the majors. And for people that live in a market served by Frontier but maybe not by the majors as much that requires them to do a lot of connections. Having a roomier seat up front might be enough to attract them, and requires very little investment for Frontier to provide.

Given that it’s really just a seat upgrade and not an upgrade in service, I’m surprised they went with a solid divider between cabins. JetBlue isn’t even doing that with BlueFirst.

I flew LAS-ORD-LAS about a couple of years ago on Frontier (my first non-AA/AS flight after hundreds of flights over the decades). The fare, even with paying for exit rows both ways was literally < 1/2 of the price AA (I don't fly on non-OneWorld carriers and UA wasn't cheap either). Since I didn't have any luggage, I felt it was at least worth a try. I'll be honest, it wasn't too bad. Now if I had to check baggage in, multiple flights, etc. then it definitely wouldn't have been worth it.

#6161. SAS Boosts Flights To These 2 Major Delta Hubs For Summer 2027

SAS is increasing flights to two major Delta Air Lines hubs as part of an extensive expansion of its summer 2027 schedule. The Scandinavian carrier will increase services from Copenhagen Airport (CPH) to Atlanta and Seattle, strengthening connections with its US partner while adding capacity across a total of seven intercontinental routes.

The November 10 announcement also includes larger Airbus aircraft, more than 20 European and Scandinavian route enhancements, and two new destinations. The expansion follows SAS's transition from Star Alliance to SkyTeam, which has brought it closer to Delta and Air France-KLM.

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) will increase from five weekly flights to a daily service from Copenhagen, representing 40% growth, while Seattle rises from four to five weekly flights. Both changes restore previously offered frequencies: SAS launched Atlanta flights in June 2024, shortly before its formal move to SkyTeam, wasting no time connecting into the alliance's busiest global hub. SAS also operates nonstop services to three other Delta hubs: Boston, Los Angeles and New York-JFK.

SAS' partnership with Delta formally began in September 2024, just days after joining the alliance, with a revised codeshare agreement. The expanded agreement covered 150 destinations in North America, as well as around 50 destinations in Northern Europe. The cooperation increased again in April 2025, with both carriers adding more connecting opportunities and reciprocal loyalty benefits. Paul Verhagen, Chief Commercial Officer at SAS, said at the time:

“We are thrilled to continue expanding our partnership with Delta, enhancing travel options between Scandinavia and North America. As a proud new member of SkyTeam Alliance, our collaboration offers great opportunities to provide seamless connectivity and benefits across our global network."

The relationship is expected to deepen further through Air France-KLM's proposed acquisition of a controlling 60.5% stake in SAS. During its November 5 earnings call, the group's CEO Benjamin Smith said the group now hopes to complete the transaction in the first quarter of 2027, subject to European Commission approval. This could eventually support SAS joining the existing Delta–Air France–KLM–Virgin Atlantic transatlantic joint venture.

Beyond Atlanta and Seattle, SAS will increase Copenhagen flights to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND), Seoul's Incheon International Airport (ICN), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) from six weekly to daily. Chicago and Mumbai will also receive more seats through aircraft upgauging, although SAS has not announced additional frequencies for these two routes.

The A350 upgauges add 34 seats per departure, with capacity rising from 266 to 300 passengers. Mumbai Airport (BOM) is particularly noteworthy, having only launched in October this year, marking SAS's return to India after 17 years. Previously operated five times weekly with the A330, the route will enter its first full summer season with larger aircraft, demonstrating the airline's longer-term ambitions in the subcontinent.

These changes precede SAS's largest-ever aircraft investment, announced in June of this year. The agreement covers up to 40 widebodies, including 18 firm Airbus A330-900 orders, two additional leased A330-900s, ten purchase rights, and up to ten additional Airbus A330-300s. The secondhand A330s will support near-term expansion, while new-generation aircraft will underpin fleet modernization. The investment has a stated list-price value exceeding $10 billion.

The carrier has put pen to paper on the largest investment in its history.

As if that wasn't enough, SAS is also strengthening its European and Scandinavian network to support Copenhagen's development as a major international connecting hub. Flights from Copenhagen to Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN) will increase from 15 to 18 daily departures, while Aarhus rises from four to five daily flights. Geneva, Barcelona and Venice will also gain significant additional capacity, improving connections between European destinations and SAS's expanding long-haul network.

Beyond these confirmed increases, SAS also plans more departures from Copenhagen to Nice, Palma de Mallorca, Porto, Bilbao and Catania, although frequencies are not yet confirmed. Stockholm will gain additional flights to Luleå, Kiruna, Milan and Madrid, while Geneva and Keflavik services will operate throughout the summer. Oslo will also see increased frequencies to Manchester, Brussels and Rome.

The expansion also introduces two new seasonal destinations from Copenhagen. Ljubljana Jože Pucnik Airport (LJU) launches June 25, operating twice-weekly until August 6 with a 122-seat Embraer E195. Menorca follows on June 30, with weekly flights until August 4 using a 180-seat Airbus A320neo. Menorca becomes SAS's third Balearic destination, while Ljubljana adds another European capital to its network. Together, the new additions reinforce Copenhagen's role as the airline's principal international hub.

#6160. New Bilt Deals With Hyatt, Marriott And Sports Team Reveal Bigger Bet On Rewards Across Your Whole Neighborhood

Bilt wants the building you live in, the hotel program you belong to, and the team you root for to get you recognized and rewarded at businesses around you. Its new Neighborhood OS and membership platform bring together merchants, housing communities, Hyatt, Marriott and professional sports teams in a much bigger play than earning points on rent. The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back. I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use. There are two pieces to the announcement: Tools for merchants. Neighborhood OS connects the reservation, payment, point of sale and loyalty systems a business already uses. The goal is to help it recognize customers, deliver benefits, bring in new business and encourage repeat visits. Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it. The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals! “Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent. Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry. We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched. Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest. Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert). And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants: Find customers who can become regulars. A restaurant with empty tables on Tuesday can reach people in nearby buildings who are deciding where to eat. Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full. Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people. Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount. There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. Bilt’s tech is better than what others have tried in the past. Here’s Bilt’s illustration of the merchant experience: The artificial intelligence component isn’t just buzz marketing. They can handle requests and coordinate actions across systems that otherwise require staff to do the work manually. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. ChenaultLyftLyftMarriott InternationalOpenTablePlentiRite AidUnited KingdomWalgreens+17 more More From View from the Wing

The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back.

I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use.

There are two pieces to the announcement:

Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it.

The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027.

Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals!

“Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS

What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent.

Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs.

The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry.

We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched.

Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest.

Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert).

And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants:

Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full.

Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people.

Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount.

There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

They want to be a middleman and they’ve done payment processing for some big landlords. Exciting. Unfortunately, their 2026 was a complete disaster – dumped by a real bank, picked up by PE who wanted pie in the sky but instead got 3 versions of a credit card in 8 months that never achieved any market penetration. On the heels of that failure they’re pulling the rug out from the only part of the credit card that offered a bit more value to consumers than they could get from reliable banks.

All that means is that the marketing dollars they put into their growth plan did not result in more growth, so the marketing dollars had to be cut off because the hockey stick growth that would have supported the charade never materialized.

Now, of course, they have PE investors that would like to make some money off of this failure. So what do they do? They have some digital infrastructure that is underutilized and that they’d like to more broadly deploy. So back to basics… meaningless puffery and branding! They’re trying to refocus on the “meh” stuff that they originally did, because when pie in the sky fails, that’s what you do. Notably absent from this announcement though are any real, meaningful partnerships for “the Neighborhood OS”. Such branding and hubris.

Anyway, good news everyone, our neighborhoods are about to be brought together like never before by Bilt’s amazing AI capabilities… you know, the ones that couldn’t even answer questions about its own program accurately? In fairness, Bilt executives couldn’t answer questions about its own program accurately, so seems harsh to blame the AI.

Enjoy the grandfathering while it lasts, folks.

Wuttt. This was supposed to be a big jetBlue announcement day. So much for that… Oof. So, they’re now pulling an Allbirds, Boom Supersonic “but, but, actually, we’re now an AI company”? Very 2024/2025 of them. I think they missed the gravy train on that one.

If Bilt and Hyatt really want to make a difference, allow their hotel bookings through Bilt to qualify for EQN like Amex FHR program does.

That will make me want to stay at Hyatts using Bilt.

This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

Re Sports teams sponsorships, hopefully they only view it as an advertising for new customers /sponsorship sort of thing. I have no interest in redeeming my points for watching overpriced US franchises.

@Too many – I think Bilt has been talking about that exactly

Remember, all of this is only worth $620, less than most other cards. Frequent Miler says so, and thye are so omniscient they don’t even need facts to prove it.

At the end of the day, loyalty programs operate within the razor-thin margins of retail. Why would these businesses fund rewards for another ecosystem instead of their own?

No amount of corporate spin can hide the obvious: Bilt bought market share with a credit card point system they certainly lost money on. Pretending it’s business genius to attract cardholders when you literally paid for them to be your customer is a choice.

“And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g., a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert).”

I love this fairy tale of “integrated rewards” where one credit seamlessly leads to another in a virtuous cycle. That is completely disconnected from how consumers actually behave. Nobody plans a night out three months in advance around stringing together a free Lyft, a free appetizer, and an ice cream.

People burn rewards when they get them or hoard them for flight. Marketers love drawing neat, circular diagrams of loyalty ecosystems, but real usage is jagged.

And sports? Live entertainment and sports are notorious for offering terrible value. At this point, it’s literally cheaper to take my girlfriend to Italy than it is to buy a decent seat at MSG against a competitor.

Hotel Loyalty? Once everyone is special, no one is.

And Grubhub? It’s the bottom of the barrel among delivery platforms. Every single party in the food delivery economy is miserable: consumers get gouged by markups and fees, drivers make pennies, and restaurants watch their margins get stripped away.

Want a real loyalty program? Become a regular at your local neighborhood spot. Get to know the owner, the bartenders, and the staff. You’ll get far more genuine hospitality, comped drinks, and a sense of community by supporting a local business than you ever will churning points.

@L3 — Bahaha… I love that you cannot let that go… L3 again… never change!

Not sure how they’ll get this to work considering every time I try to use Bilt Checkout at the handful of places listed in the app I get a confused stare

#6157. United Airlines Pilot Couldn’t Fly After A Stroke—His Union Urged Removal, And His Military Bias Suit Failed

A United Airlines pilot left for military duty in September 2001, planning to come back two years later. Instead, he was furloughed, suffered a stroke, lost his medical clearance and eventually learned that his own union had recommended removing him from the airline’s seniority list. Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions. United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003. Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force. On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke. United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open. His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019. United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September. In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline. Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012. In January 2019, Bumpus sought to return and obtain medical leave to preserve his employment while resolving his medical certification. United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired. He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority. Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023. He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches: United owed him reemployment after military service. This included his argument that it should accommodate his medical condition through leave or an appropriate alternative position. United treated him worse because of his military service. He pointed to other pilots who received leave or returned with their seniority intact. I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role. But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway. What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military. He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. The judge assumed, for purposes of deciding the case, that Bumpus was right about the 2019 deadline. Even with that assumption, he hadn’t shown military bias. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias. The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to. Twenty-five years after that leave began, William Michael Bumpus has lost his military discrimination lawsuit. On November 6, a federal judge in Chicago ruled that he hadn’t produced evidence that his military service motivated United’s decisions.

United hired Bumpus in June 2000 and assigned him to Denver. He took approved leave in September 2001 to serve with the Air Force Reserve’s 706th Fighter Squadron, expecting to return in September 2003.

Then United furloughed him in 2002, along with many other pilots. The airline struggled after 9/11 and went through a prolonged bankruptcy. According to his amended complaint, he was at Barksdale Air Force Base when a United supervisor called. He explained that he’d stay employed by the Air Force.

On September 5, 2006, Bumpus suffered a stroke while on active duty. He was hospitalized and lost the medical certification he needed to fly. The record establishes that this happened during military service, but there’s no indication military service caused the stroke.

United recalled him in May 2007. He accepted and told the airline about his medical condition. He didn’t request leave, although the recall offered that option. In January 2008, United told him he’d remain furloughed, with his recall rights expiring in March 2012 if he didn’t obtain medical clearance. He couldn’t fly for United, but the airline was still holding his space open.

His employee record showed United returning him to active status and furloughing him again on March 2, 2009. A new furlough could start a fresh ten-year recall period, extending his right to return until March 2019.

United offered another recall in 2012, and he requested a military deferment, which the airline acknowledged. His military service ended in March 2013. He still lacked medical clearance and bypassed another recall that September.

In 2015, United’s furlough return coordinator told him he’d looked further into the case and confirmed the March 2019 deadline.

Then, in 2017, the Air Line Pilots Association reviewed irregularities in United’s seniority list. The union recommended removing Bumpus. United agreed, concluding that his recall rights had expired in 2012.

In January 2019, Bumpus sought to return and obtain medical leave to preserve his employment while resolving his medical certification. United initially told him his recall rights ran until March 2019. Days later, the airline reversed itself: its review with the union showed those rights had already expired.

He finally obtained a first class medical certificate in June 2020, nearly fourteen years after the stroke. United had offered to consider him as a new hire, but he didn’t apply. He wanted his original seniority.

Bumpus pursued a grievance and, in 2021, sued United and the union to obtain access to arbitration. The union wouldn’t take his case forward. He eventually got an arbitration hearing, but his grievance was dismissed as untimely in March 2023.

He filed a lawsuit in June 2023, seeking reinstatement with full seniority, lost pay and other damages. He alleged that United accommodated other pilots and brought back 111 pilots without military service while refusing to restore him. His claims under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act took two different approaches:

I’ve covered an American Airlines case involving a reservist who couldn’t legally fly but was nevertheless entitled to prompt reemployment in an appropriate role.

But Bumpus lost his reemployment claims in May 2025. The judge found that his absence from September 2001 to his accepted recall in May 2007 exceeded the law’s five-year service limit. He argued that time spent on economic furlough shouldn’t count: United wasn’t offering him work during those years anyway.

What remained was discrimination. Bumpus needed evidence that his military service was at least one reason for United’s actions. His argument about leave ran into a basic problem: he hadn’t requested it in 2007. He also hadn’t shown that the other pilots received leave without asking. United’s treatment of those pilots didn’t establish that it denied him the same benefit because he served in the military.

He did seek medical accommodation in 2019. By then, however, United and the union believed his recall rights had expired. The judge assumed, for purposes of deciding the case, that Bumpus was right about the 2019 deadline. Even with that assumption, he hadn’t shown military bias. United also removed two pilots with no military background after concluding their recall rights had expired, too. So even if United miscalculated, it wasn’t motivated by anti-military bias.

The pilot here wasn’t punished for his service. He couldn’t fly for United for years and they held out a spot for him anyway. It’s a complicated case that generated contradictory answers about exactly what his rights were under a union contract and government requirements. The union agreed he should lose his seniority. His medical clearance eventually expired again in 2024. He last flew for United a quarter century ago, and he can’t currently fly even if he wanted to.

#6156. Lufthansa’s First Airbus A350-1000 Has Arrived: 299.5 Seats, Four Cabins, Munich Routes

In 2023, Lufthansa Group placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000 — the order was initially for 10 frames, before being increased to 15 frames the following year. The Lufthansa Group is undergoing a massive long haul fleet modernization at the moment, with both Airbus and Boeing planes on the way.

Along those lines, the first Lufthansa A350-1000 has just joined the carrier’s fleet (in a dazzling livery no less), so let’s cover all the details, including the routes the plane will fly, how the plane is configured, etc.

Between late 2026 and 2030, Lufthansa is taking delivery of 15 Airbus A350-1000s. This is only one of several aircraft types the airline is acquiring, as it’s also taking delivery of Airbus A350-900s, Boeing 787-9s, and (eventually) Boeing 777-9s.

The first A350-1000 has just been delivered today, with three more planes expected to be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of the year. This first plane even features the special 100th anniversary livery, as Lufthansa has seven of these flying, with one representing each fleet type.

The first plane has the registration code D-AIFA, and is named “Deutschland” (since Lufthansa names all of its planes). This is a special plane for another reason, as it’s also the 700th aircraft that Airbus has delivered to Lufthansa Group. How gorgeous is this plane?!?

Here’s how Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Hub Manager for Munich, describes this:

“We are proud that the Airbus A350-1000—Airbus’s most modern long-haul aircraft—is coming to Munich. The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability. Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: The A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?

We’ve known that the Airbus A350-1000s will get the new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris first class and Allegris business class. So, what can we expect in terms of the configuration? The A350-1000 features 300 seats, spread across four cabins, as follows:

As a point of comparison, the A350-900 (the non-stretched version of the plane) features 267 seats, as follows:

So the stretched version has 11 more business class seats, 11 more premium economy seats, and 11 more economy seats (11 more seats across three cabins, what a funny coincidence). The airline is still maintaining only one row of first class, which is kind of “bleh.”

You can find the Lufthansa A350-1000 seat map here.

Lufthansa Airbus A350-1000s will all be stationed in Munich (MUC), which is where Lufthansa bases all of its A350s. The first of these planes is entering long haul commercial service as of early December 2026.

Specifically, as of December 3, 2026, the A350-1000 will fly between Munich and Tokyo Haneda (HND), with the next two destinations being Shanghai (PVG) and Singapore (SIN), and those services expected to launch within weeks, though the schedule hasn’t yet been updated to reflect that.

Note that initially the flights won’t be operated by the A350-1000 daily, so there will be alternating service with the A350-900. It’s interesting that the initial route isn’t to North America, where a single plane could do a same day turn, and continuously stay in service. but I guess there’s enough commonality between the A350-900 and A350-1000, so it’s not a big deal.

As far as US destinations go, it’s expected that Chicago (ORD) and Newark (EWR) will be the first two cities to see the new plane, though there’s no exact timeline for that yet.

In 2023, Lufthansa placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000, and the first of these planes has just been delivered, and will enter service in early December 2026. The plane features 300 seats across four cabins, though still only expect one row of first class seats. The Munich-based plane will initially fly to Tokyo, Shanghai, and Singapore. I must say, Lufthansa knocked it out of the park with its centennial livery, and I can’t wait to see this plane flying.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-1000 deliveries?

#6154. Airport Lounges Are Packed—Travelers Demand $5,000 Annual Credit Card Fees To Keep The Masses Out

Airport lounges are so crowded that travelers are demanding $200 admission prices and $5,000 annual credit card fees to keep the “untouchables” out, arguing that the “true lounge caste” has been driven into the concourse while everyone else crowds around the buffet. There are also lounges where the line outside and the crowd inside make the benefit nearly worthless. Paying for somewhere comfortable to sit, and then being unable to find a seat, has become a really legitimate complaint – even if it’s mixed with real snobbery because it’s the ‘other’ people who shouldn’t be in there. “Premium” travel experience before 10am on a Sunday https://t.co/13PniAuksG — David Slotnick (@David_Slotnick) November 8, 2026 Status anxiety places airline lounges belong alongside BMWs, remote work, and ski trips as things that have lost their cachet as access spread. They’re still aspirational to the people getting in, while the people already inside are unhappy that increased access has lowered their relative status. View wyatt.today’s post on Twitter The original poster’s follow-up invokes the tens of thousands of his employer’s dollars he spends on flights, then uses a racial slur for other guests. It’s no longer about finding empty space inside. But most people just want a chance to use the benefit they’re paying for and maybe a snack without standing in line in the terminal like a schmuck to get an $895 ‘free’ drink. Wanting Quiet Space Isn’t Elitist One reply argues that a lounge defeats its purpose when it gets too crowded. It may still have food, a shower, or an airline agent to help when your flight gets delayed or cancels. But the core value proposition is escape from the terminal. I often just want a place to open my laptop without balancing it on my knees. And then having frictionless access to a snack, and the ability to run into the washroom without bringing all my stuff with me, are cherries on top. Nobel laureate James Buchanan’s theory of clubs explains this well. Sharing a facility spreads its costs across more people. Eventually, adding people creates enough congestion to make the experience worse. The membership and the size of the facility have to be considered together. There need to be access limits to preserve the value proposition of the facility. But since most people don’t use the space most of the time, it’s perceived option value that they’re purchasing and it continues to drive premium credit card acquisition and adoption. Lounges Got Better, And People Started Using Them Differently I’ve written about the claim that airport lounge culture represents American decline. The nostaglic view is just wrong. I remember ginger ale and Goldfish crackers, a photocopier in the Admirals Club, and packaged Tillamook cheese in United’s Red Carpet Clubs. Today’s better lounges offer actual meals and craft cocktails. When I visited Chase’s new Dallas–Fort Worth lounge, I found the best food inside a bank lounge that isn’t a Capital One Landing. Plus they have whiskey tastings, and facial treatments. The space is 18,000 square feet. These spaces are no longer just a room with seating, snacks and a fax machine. The same improvements help explain why lounges fill up. People go for the food People who might have stopped in to check e-mail now plan to eat a meal. They come more often and stay longer. A better lounge becomes a destination in its own right. The travel mix has changed. Traditional managed business travel is a smaller part of the story. Premium leisure travelers, families, and people combining work with a trip use the same spaces. A Monday – Thursday consultant arriving just before boarding and a family building in a generous airport buffer spend very different amounts of time. Credit cards have expanded access. That brings in more people, including travelers who wouldn’t buy a separate airline club membership. Uncertain security waits get people to the airport earlier. If security might take ten minutes or an hour, you allow for the hour. When it takes ten minutes, you’ve suddenly got time to spend. Even without an increase in the average security wait, greater uncertainty can mean more time in the airport. I laid out these problems for Delta years ago. Their more substantial food draws people in and keeps them there. And Delta doesn’t just admit customers with its own premium card – American Express Platinum cardmembers flying Delta can enter, too. Platinum’s standard allotment is now 10 visits and Delta Reserve’s is 15, with a spending route to unlimited access. Delta also limits entry before an originating flight to three hours prior to scheduled departure, with an exception for connections. A three-hour entry window still leaves plenty of time for a long visit. And if everyone arrives before the same bank of departures, an empty room earlier in the day doesn’t help. The number of people holding an eligible card isn’t the only number that matters. Double the average length of a visit, with the same flow of arrivals, and you double the average number of people occupying the lounge. I recently catalogued 70 new and expanded lounge projects. More space helps, but a new lounge also attracts people who previously skipped the experience. I’d underscore that which lounges we’re talking about matters a great deal. Spending $895 for a Platinum Card doesn’t on its own signal discernment, although I their Salt Lake lounge is quite nice. Capital One’s Landings at Washington National and LaGuardia offer genuinely good food and reservations. You enter and are shown to a table. That’s a totally different experience. You Could Buy Your Way Into Lounges In The 1960s, Too One commenter remembers the 1990s as a time when people earned their way in by flying. But American Airlines started selling lounge memberships in 1967, at $25 a year or $250 for life. Before that, their sales department handed out memberships. Paid lounge access was a function of the civil rights era – a nondiscriminatory way to determine who could enter. The claim that credit card lounges are bad while airline lounges are good doesn’t make sense. I’d happily choose a good Chase or Capital One lounge over plenty of airline clubs. And finding quiet lounges overseas doesn’t mean most overseas lounges are quiet. Have you ever tried to enter a Priority Pass lounge at Heathrow? Comfort Can Spread Even When Status Can’t The discussion of aspiration is revealing. Some people feel that accessibility is the inverse of aspiration – that’s true if what you’re aspiring to is being above other people. But you can also just aspire to a more comfortable trip, get it, and be pleased that other people can get it too. A product can also become less distinctive to its old customers while becoming an attainable aspiration for new ones. The people entering and the people complaining aren’t necessarily the same people. That’s why the comparison to remote work is revealing – someone getting to work from home doesn’t take away the time you save on your commute working from home. Treating it as a status symbol entails a tradeoff (‘when everyone has status, nobody does’). I’m glad more people can have a better trip. I also want the benefit I’ve paid for to be usable. I don’t usually bother with Centurion lounges, they aren’t as nice as Capital One and Chase lounges in many airports and there are too many people waiting to get in. When there’s a choice, I’ll pick elsewhere. But some of those Chase (Las Vegas! Phoenix!) and Capital One lounges (Denver!) can make the wait not worth the squeeze, too. Banks are selling more access than they can deliver. Sometimes I’ll just take the restaurant in the terminal. Of course most banks stopped paying for Priority Passs swipes at restaurants – which would be fair enough if they could accommodate travelers in their own lounges. Paying for somewhere comfortable to sit, and then being unable to find a seat, has become a really legitimate complaint – even if it’s mixed with real snobbery because it’s the ‘other’ people who shouldn’t be in there.

Platinum’s standard allotment is now 10 visits and Delta Reserve’s is 15, with a spending route to unlimited access. Delta also limits entry before an originating flight to three hours prior to scheduled departure, with an exception for connections. A three-hour entry window still leaves plenty of time for a long visit. And if everyone arrives before the same bank of departures, an empty room earlier in the day doesn’t help. The number of people holding an eligible card isn’t the only number that matters. Double the average length of a visit, with the same flow of arrivals, and you double the average number of people occupying the lounge. I recently catalogued 70 new and expanded lounge projects. More space helps, but a new lounge also attracts people who previously skipped the experience. I’d underscore that which lounges we’re talking about matters a great deal. Spending $895 for a Platinum Card doesn’t on its own signal discernment, although I their Salt Lake lounge is quite nice. Capital One’s Landings at Washington National and LaGuardia offer genuinely good food and reservations. You enter and are shown to a table. That’s a totally different experience. You Could Buy Your Way Into Lounges In The 1960s, Too One commenter remembers the 1990s as a time when people earned their way in by flying. But American Airlines started selling lounge memberships in 1967, at $25 a year or $250 for life. Before that, their sales department handed out memberships. Paid lounge access was a function of the civil rights era – a nondiscriminatory way to determine who could enter. The claim that credit card lounges are bad while airline lounges are good doesn’t make sense. I’d happily choose a good Chase or Capital One lounge over plenty of airline clubs. And finding quiet lounges overseas doesn’t mean most overseas lounges are quiet. Have you ever tried to enter a Priority Pass lounge at Heathrow? Comfort Can Spread Even When Status Can’t The discussion of aspiration is revealing. Some people feel that accessibility is the inverse of aspiration – that’s true if what you’re aspiring to is being above other people. But you can also just aspire to a more comfortable trip, get it, and be pleased that other people can get it too. A product can also become less distinctive to its old customers while becoming an attainable aspiration for new ones. The people entering and the people complaining aren’t necessarily the same people. That’s why the comparison to remote work is revealing – someone getting to work from home doesn’t take away the time you save on your commute working from home. Treating it as a status symbol entails a tradeoff (‘when everyone has status, nobody does’). I’m glad more people can have a better trip. I also want the benefit I’ve paid for to be usable. I don’t usually bother with Centurion lounges, they aren’t as nice as Capital One and Chase lounges in many airports and there are too many people waiting to get in. When there’s a choice, I’ll pick elsewhere. But some of those Chase (Las Vegas! Phoenix!) and Capital One lounges (Denver!) can make the wait not worth the squeeze, too. Banks are selling more access than they can deliver. Sometimes I’ll just take the restaurant in the terminal. Of course most banks stopped paying for Priority Passs swipes at restaurants – which would be fair enough if they could accommodate travelers in their own lounges. The membership and the size of the facility have to be considered together. There need to be access limits to preserve the value proposition of the facility. But since most people don’t use the space most of the time, it’s perceived option value that they’re purchasing and it continues to drive premium credit card acquisition and adoption.

Plus they have whiskey tastings, and facial treatments. The space is 18,000 square feet. These spaces are no longer just a room with seating, snacks and a fax machine. The same improvements help explain why lounges fill up. People go for the food People who might have stopped in to check e-mail now plan to eat a meal. They come more often and stay longer. A better lounge becomes a destination in its own right. The travel mix has changed. Traditional managed business travel is a smaller part of the story. Premium leisure travelers, families, and people combining work with a trip use the same spaces. A Monday – Thursday consultant arriving just before boarding and a family building in a generous airport buffer spend very different amounts of time. Credit cards have expanded access. That brings in more people, including travelers who wouldn’t buy a separate airline club membership. Uncertain security waits get people to the airport earlier. The folks with lounge access through their employer are the problem! I pay the annual fee for my Chase Sapphire Reserve card and have never seen a line at a Chase lounge in Philly or Boston but have seen the Centurion lounge lines. Why? Most of those folks are using a business AmEx card paid for by their employer. If they had to pay that annual fee, I suspect there’d be no lines. That comment about a $5,000 annual fee is probably from someone whose employer pays it!

With EU261 in place in the U.S., lounges would rightfully accept everyone, at any time.

Good one, Matt. Anyway, I think Gary is right in his thinking. The lounges have gotten much better in their quality over the years. But travel has changed, and I think the crowding issue is a function of those changes, fueled by Americans becoming much wealthier with more to spend on travel, while at the same time, post-COVID, travel habits have leaned towards arriving earlier at the airport and having longer connections.

I meant to add that the lines at Delta Sky Club can be skipped if you are in F on DL. There is often some good lounge that you can go to that is crowded but not overcrowded, so long as you are in long-haul J (Polaris, DL One, Virgin) – except at LHR T5.

Another thing to consider is the cost of eating a meal at the airport for family versus getting a card with lounge or priority club access and having a free meal before the flight.

“Travelers” demand $5K credit card fees? Really? TRAVELERS?

And who is this source that speaks for all travelers? Is there a union for travelers that I should have joined that is speaking for me? Was there a massive survey of travelers that collected this data.

Or by “travelers” we don’t actually mean travelers — we mean one, maybe a couple, social media “influencers”.

Last 12 months: 5 RT to Europe on AA Flagship Biz at $5-$10K per trip. That’s 10 visits to Terminal D DFW Flagship Lounge. (Yes Gary, I agree the food is getting marginally better and I have yet to place order or eat in private dining.) Space is only getting worse.

I don’t get the whole lounge thing. Get to your departure gate 30 minutes before departure and be on your way. Should you arrive early find a quiet gate and open your laptop.

@Matt — I wish. EU261 provides excellent basic consumer protections, not “VIP” lounge membership. For a “premium” airport lounge experience, please consider the Delta One lounge (now at JFK, LAX, BOS, SEA, but not ATL, because those suckers at HQ are fortress hub hostages…)

And the occupancy rates on the private suites at the CSR LGA lounge are….?

I believe the biggest problem is the airlines haven’t added enough lounge space to keep up with increased premium cabin demand. Airlines could help by adding restrictions on who has access to lounges until they have constructed adequate space.

Enforce a jacket and tie dress code. You’ll instantly remove 95%+ of people.

Lounges have become entirely too desirable, what with halfway decent food and liquor I remember the JKF Sky Club offering Chex Mix with jug wine and a cheap Scotch universally rated as one of the worst whiskies ever bottled. The place was quiet and empty.

Well played Matt – Add that to the irony of the left, they are usually the most classist people when it comes to put their own skin in the game. It’s always the other ppl pocket they want to grab and unfortunately that’s why there so many of these parasites in politics.

Amateurs call for more-exclusive airport lounges. Professionals call for more-exclusive airports.

Haven’t had the pleasure of trying them myself, but those José Andrés tapas in the C1 lounges always look gorgeous!

“Status anxiety places airline lounges belong alongside BMWs, remote work, and ski trips as things that have lost their cachet as access spread. ”

The same with “elite” status in loyalty programs. So many more people with status despite dwindling returns. I keep thinking people will eventually wake up. But then when I see those long lines outside of lounges I realize humanity is doomed.

when we flew to UK in August the sfo AA lounge was absolutely ghetto – actually witnessed 2 women fighting – food & trash all over the floor – children eating buffet food w/ their fingers & spitting some back into the bowls –

If this is true….. those Elitists can fly private and not worry about the slaves beneath them!

“Sharing a facility spreads its costs across more people.”

“Eventually, adding people creates enough congestion to make the experience worse.”

And…”Nobody goes there anymore. It’s too crowded.” Yogi

A thought just struck me. I thought we go to the airport to fly a plane to a destination, for work or pleasure. The planes I fly offer decent food and drink.

Frankly, this obsession with lounges/clubs, to me, is just pretentious.

The solution would be for companies to retain the benefits of employees flying. And certainly not paying for any cc, except basic ones.

For all those that want better clubs for me, not thee, fly private.

Oh, and by the way, Gary, isn’t you who writes two or three times a year, there is no reason to waste your time by showing up at the airport early. As you say, you are wasting productive time.

Lounge demand is also a function of the degraded onboard experience in coach and even first class. You know you’re going to suffer on the plane so grabbing a drink and some food before flying is more important than it was 20 years ago. That’s another, possibly equal, core value proposition.

Nothing says “living the dream” quite like intentionally extending your stay at an airport so you can sit in a room that is marginally less depressing than the rest of the airport.

I have access to three different lounge programs and have used them approximately once. This is because my airport philosophy is simple: airports are not destinations. They are obstacles. The objective is to spend as little time there as possible.

The only time you’ll find me lingering at an airport is when an airline has involuntarily altered my schedule. At that point, I’ll grab a table at a decent restaurant and order exactly what I want instead of fighting over the last mini quiche and a warm can of Diet Coke.

If you’re flying enough to earn lounge status, or you’re already sitting up front and getting lounge access included, I genuinely don’t understand the excitement over free snacks. The math simply isn’t computing.

Then again, I also walk right past Starbucks every day. So perhaps I just lack the refined appreciation for overpaying for things I don’t actually need while convincing myself it’s an elite experience.

#6153. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

If you’ve flown ANA’s new 777s, what was your experience like?
