#6152. Alaska Airlines Launches Invite-Only Global Concierge Status To Rival US Big Three

Alaska Airlines has introduced Atmos Global Concierge, an invitation-only elite status program that recognizes its most valuable customers with personalized travel assistance and exclusive benefits. The new offering sits above the existing Atmos Rewards Titanium tier and brings the Seattle-based carrier closer to American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines, all of which operate their own invitation-only loyalty programs. Invitations began reaching selected Atmos Rewards members on November 9, 2026, with membership currently extending through December 31, 2027. The initiative comes as Alaska continues to expand its international network and strengthen its position in the premium travel market.

The new status is a curious case because Alaska has not published qualification requirements or established a publicly accessible application process. Instead, the airline appears to be selecting travelers based on their overall value to its business, with early reports suggesting that expensive international business class bookings could play an important role. Recipients are also being offered complimentary Titanium status, alongside a collection of services intended to make long-haul journeys more convenient. Although the program remains in its early stages, it represents another important development in Alaska's evolving loyalty strategy.

Atmos Global Concierge provides invited members with access to a dedicated support team responsible for assisting them throughout their journeys. According to information shared by recipients on Reddit, the benefits include proactive flight monitoring, assistance during travel disruptions, and a next-flight guarantee intended to help passengers reach their destinations when their original itineraries are disrupted. Members can also receive arrival assistance at selected long-haul destinations across Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Another benefit is car transfers at London Heathrow Airport (LHR) for passengers with tight connections.

The reported package also includes upgrade priority above regular Titanium members, particularly on international flights, alongside complimentary CLEAR+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. These benefits combine airport assistance, ground transportation, and additional travel privileges rather than focusing exclusively on earning more points or accessing airport lounges. According to One Mile at a Time, recipients can retain their new status through December 31, 2027. Alaska has also confirmed the broader purpose of the initiative, stating the following to Simple Flying:

“Atmos™ Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most. Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences. Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows.”

The introduction of Global Concierge places Alaska alongside the three largest US network carriers in offering exclusive recognition to selected customers. American Airlines operates ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has Delta 360, while United Airlines offers Global Services. These programs are generally reserved for travelers considered especially valuable to their respective airlines, with spending patterns, premium cabin bookings, and corporate travel relationships often believed to influence selection. Qualification criteria are typically confidential, making invitations hard to predict even for frequent flyers.

Early reactions from Atmos Rewards members suggest that Alaska may be prioritizing the value of individual bookings rather than simply rewarding the highest number of status points. Reports shared on Reddit indicate that some recipients regularly purchase international business class tickets, while other members with substantial status-point balances have not received invitations. This suggests the airline may be trying to attract customers who might otherwise spend heavily with competing international carriers.

The distinction between Global Concierge and conventional elite status is that it appears to emphasize personalized assistance rather than simply offering additional mileage bonuses or airport privileges. For passengers traveling internationally, having an airline team monitor their itineraries and arrange alternatives during disruptions could be very valuable. A missed connection at a major European hub, for example, can create significant complications when passengers have connecting flights operated by different carriers. Alaska's reported Heathrow transfer benefit also indicates that the airline is looking beyond its own aircraft operations to improve the overall travel experience.

The initiative also reflects a broader effort to retain premium customers as Alaska expands its international operations. Following its acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines, the company has gained access to a substantially broader network and greater opportunities to compete for long-haul passengers. Recognizing travelers who regularly purchase expensive international tickets could help strengthen loyalty as Alaska develops additional services and competes with established global airlines.

The new program brings a lot to the table.

Alaska has described Global Concierge as a beta program designed to develop new ways to recognize its most loyal customers as its global network grows. In a comment explaining the initiative, the airline said the new offering supplements existing Atmos Rewards benefits with personalized support, proactive travel monitoring, exclusive privileges, and curated experiences. The company also highlighted the importance of having a dedicated team available throughout each member's journey, particularly when unexpected travel complications arise. This suggests that Alaska sees the program as more than another loyalty designation, positioning it instead as a premium service offering that could evolve as the airline gathers feedback.

However, several questions about the program remain unanswered. Alaska has not disclosed how customers are selected, whether it will issue invitations regularly, or what spending levels might make someone eligible. The precise conditions surrounding the reported next-flight guarantee and Heathrow transfers also remain unclear. Furthermore, the benefits currently reported by members do not indicate whether Global Concierge will add lounge access, separate boarding privileges, or improved award availability.

The move nevertheless arrives at an important time for Alaska Airlines. Its expanding international ambitions require the carrier to compete not only through fares and destinations but also through the quality of its premium passenger experience. Atmos Global Concierge gives Alaska another tool to attract high-value travelers who might otherwise favor the US Big Three when booking expensive international journeys. Whether the beta program eventually becomes a permanent fixture of Atmos Rewards remains to be seen, but its introduction signals that Alaska intends to compete more directly for the most lucrative segment of the US airline loyalty market.

#6150. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

There’s no card that earns more for ongoing spending than the Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees). It’s a $495 annual fee card, and that I think that easily makes sense if you’re spending $25,000 or more a year on the card (that’s just a little over $2,000 a month).

But not everyone is going to invest in an expensive card. I talk most about products like this, and the $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees).

I think it’s really worth looking at mid-tier cards, also. Something more expensive than the no annual fee products, where you can still do quite well, but if you’re willing to invest a little but you can get outsized return.

I love Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (See rates and fees) for lounge access, and I think it’s easily worth the $395 annual fee considering it’s effectively rebated in value by the $300 annual credit for bookings through Capital One Travel and 10,000 bonus miles (equal to $100 towards travel) every year, starting on your first anniversary.

But if you don’t want to spend that much on an annual fee then Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (See rates and fees) still earns at least 2X miles on all purchases and they’re transferrable points. It has a $95 annual fee.

Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (See rates and fees) has an offer to earn 100k bonus points after you spend $8,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening.

What’s great is earning 3x (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases) on travel, shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, advertising purchases made with social media sites and search engines each account anniversary year.

It has the same points transfer partners as Chase Sapphire Reserve®, for a lot less money, and a lot of the points-earning for spend. And if you have some of the no annaul fee Chase cards, you can move the points from those cards over to Ink Business Preferred and then transfer them to airlines and hotel programs.

Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) This isn’t the ultra-premium Strate Elite. But you still earn 60,000 bonus ThankYou® Points after spending $4,000 in the first 3 months of account opening.

Where it shines is as a tool to earn for your spending at the $95 annual fee price point: Earn 10 Points per $1 spent on Hotels, Car Rentals, and Attractions booked on CitiTravel.com; Earn 3 Points per $1 on Air Travel and Other Hotel Purchases, at Restaurants, Supermarkets, Gas and EV Charging Stations; Earn 1 Point per $1 spent on all other purchases.

And points transfer to American Airlines AAdvantage, here’s the full list of partners:

Wells Fargo Autograph Journey is a sleeper because it’s a $95 annual fee card that earns 5x on hotels, 4x on airlines, and 3x on restaurants and other travel. That means it still bonuses Airbnb and cruises, which Sapphire Reserve does not. And they give you a $50 annual statement credit with a $50+ airline purchase each year, cutting the effective cost of that annual fee.

Where the card isn’t as strong is points transfers. They’ve promised more, but that’s happened very slowly. They transfer to the IAG Avios programs (Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia) as well as Air France KLM, Cathay Pacific, JetBlue, Virgin, Wyndham and Choice.

Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) is a $95 annual fee card that will earn up to 1.25X points on rent and mortgage payments with no transaction fee.

It’s great for card spending because it earns 3X on your choice of grocery (up to $25K/year) or dining. Your 3X category choice remains in effect for the entire calendar year. It also earns 2X points on travel. And it comes with a $100 Bilt Travel Hotel credit. Applied twice a year, as $50 statement credits, for qualifying Bilt Travel Portal hotel bookings.

The reason this is so strong is that, combined with points for rent or mortgage, you can be earning more than 4 points per dollar in your chosen category and these are the most valuable points and Bilt runs the biggest transfer bonuses. They partner with programs like Hyatt, United, Southwest, Alaska, and Japan Airlines. You don’t have to spend $395, $795 or $895 to earn valuable rewards. Which one of these works best for you depends on what your spend pattern looks like. Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card is probably best if you’re in a position to get a small business card. Wells Fargo Autograph Journey is great for heavy travel spend, if their transfer partners work for you. Citi Strata Premier® Card probably offers the best return for the way most people spend. While the Bilt Obsidian Card has the most potential upside if you play your hand well. There are just weeks left in 2026, and if you haven't quite reached the United MileagePlus elite status level you're hoping to secure for 2027, the clock is ticking.

From earning bonus Premier qualifying points with the right credit card to taking a last-minute flight, here are five ways to close the status gap before Dec. 31.

United's elite status qualification year runs from Jan. 1 through Dec. 31. Status earned in 2026 is valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

To qualify, you must fly at least four flights operated by United or United Express and meet one of two thresholds: a combination of Premier Qualifying Flights and PQPs or a higher PQP-only requirement.

You can check your progress in United's Premier Status Tracker, including how your upcoming flights will count toward qualification.

Some United credit cards offer bonus PQPs toward status as part of their welcome offers, in addition to redeemable United miles.

For example, the (see rates and fees) is currently offering 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 redeemable United bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

The card has a $350 introductory annual fee.

It's still possible to get bonus PQPs in 2026 as part of a new cardmember bonus on select United credit cards, but you should act quickly.

The good news is you can earn PQPs through everyday spending on United credit cards. The bad news is that most United cards earn them at a relatively slow rate of 1 PQP for every $20 spent.

That means $1,000 in purchases on most United cards would earn you just 50 PQPs.

However, the (see rates and fees) earns PQPs faster than the other personal United cards, at a rate of 1 PQP for every $15 spent. So, that same $1,000 in purchases would earn you about 66 PQPs with that card.

Every little bit helps, especially if you're close to your next status level.

Related: Why I charged $50,000 on my United card to earn status

If you already have United flights booked before the end of 2026, you may be able to earn additional PQPs by upgrading your seats.

Purchasing Economy Plus seats, United's preferred seating or paid upgrades to first class can earn 1 PQP per dollar spent (excluding taxes and fees).

You can also earn 1 PQP for every 100 MileagePlus miles redeemed for eligible seat upgrades on United and United Express flights.

Just remember that PQPs from upgrades purchased separately from your original ticket may post separately after you fly, so keep an eye on your account.

Related: What it's like in United's new Elevated Polaris business class

One of the most obvious ways to close the gap toward United elite status is to book another flight (or two) before the end of the year as part of a modern-day mileage run. Unlike in the old days, how far you fly doesn't matter if you're on United for status. It only matters how much you spend.

Ideally, you're going somewhere fun to see a friend, see some attractions or have a great meal. But if you turn around and don't leave the airport before your next flight, you won't be the first — or last — status-seeker to do so. I've certainly done it when I needed a few more segments at the very end of the year.

If you're chasing PQFs, remember that you generally earn one for each eligible flight segment on United, United Express or partner airlines.

For United-operated flights, you'll generally earn 1 PQP per dollar spent on eligible base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges, excluding government taxes and fees. You can see the estimated PQPs and PQFs a flight will earn when selecting a fare during booking.

If you need a lot of United PQPs and want to take this to the next level, it is possible to earn PQPs at a faster rate with some United partners. You can learn all about that strategy here.

Finally, if you have an upcoming United flight, you may be able to purchase additional PQPs through United's Premier Accelerator program.

To check, open an existing reservation and look for the Award Accelerator option, which lets you purchase additional redeemable miles.

Depending on your reservation, you may also see a Premier Accelerator option that lets you purchase PQPs along with redeemable miles, as shown below.

This isn't usually a cheap way to earn status, but it can be useful if you're just short of your goal and don't want to take another flight.

United is making some big changes to elite status qualification beginning in 2027, including eliminating the PQF-plus-PQP qualification pathway and raising the PQP-only requirement for Premier 1K.

That means earning status could get harder for some United travelers next year.

If you expect to rely heavily on United credit card spending to earn PQPs toward status, as I do, there's another reason to consider getting a United card before the end of 2026.

If you have an eligible United card by Dec. 31, 2026, you'll get a 5% PQP boost in 2027. For example, if you earned Platinum status in 2026, you'll get a 900-PQP boost to start 2027.

And remember, the earns PQPs faster than United's other personal cards, so it might be the best choice if every PQP is going to count.

It also currently offers an increased welcome bonus of 90,000 miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, an additional 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

But no matter what United status level you are going for or how you plan to get there, just remember that all of your activities must be completed by Dec. 31, 2026, to count toward status this year.

#6147. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?

#6145. Premium Economy On US Airlines: How The Big 3 Actually Compare

Demand for premium air travel is growing as passengers are increasingly prioritizing comfort when booking flights. According to consumer research, around 21% of travelers now consider physical comfort a deciding factor when allocating their holiday budgets. In response to this growing demand, airlines are investing heavily in their premium products. However, business and first class tickets remain expensive for many travelers. This is where premium economy comes in.

The cabin offers passengers more comfort and additional amenities than standard economy without the considerably higher cost of business class. In recent years, its popularity has been growing. In fact, industry data shows that the share of travelers choosing premium economy has increased from 16% to 20% year over year. Many airlines have been investing in this cabin, and the three largest US carriers, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines, are no exception. In this guide, we will explore how their products compare.

It is no secret to anyone that US legacy carriers were relatively slow to enter the premium economy market. For much of the 2010s, these airlines relied on extra-legroom economy products rather than introducing a separate premium economy cabin. In fact, this approach worked well in the domestic market, but several European and Asian airlines had already taken a different direction. They began offering dedicated premium economy cabins that featured wider seats, more legroom, and a distinct onboard service.

Therefore, to remain competitive, all three US airlines introduced their own premium economy products. American Airlines was the first major US carrier to offer a dedicated premium economy cabin, introducing the product on its Boeing 787-9 aircraft in 2016. United Airlines and Delta Air Lines subsequently followed, launching Premium Plus and Premium Select, respectively.

So, how do their products compare? In terms of seating, the three airlines offer fairly similar experiences, at least on paper. All three generally provide around 38 inches of seat pitch, which measures the distance between corresponding points on successive rows of seats. Seat widths are also comparable, typically ranging from approximately 18.5 to 19 inches, depending on the airline and aircraft type.

Overall, seat pitch is standardized at 38 inches (96.5 cm) across all aircraft types, while seat width ranges from 18.5 inches (47 cm) to 19 inches (48.3 cm). Screen sizes, however, vary by seat model. Aircraft equipped with Collins MiQ seats feature 11.5-inch (29.2 cm) screens, while the newer Boeing 787-9s featuring Recaro R5 seats offer larger 13.3-inch (33.8 cm) displays.

On eligible international flights, the Dallas/Fort Worth-based airline also offers chef-inspired meals and complimentary beer, wine, and spirits when full drink service is available. In addition, passengers on long-haul flights also receive an amenity kit including some skincare and basic travel essentials. Overall, the experience is the same as economy but with a thorough upgrade.

United Airlines currently takes the lead, but Delta and United continue to offer passengers compelling premium economy products.

Now let’s take a look at United Airlines’ premium economy seats, which it markets as “United Premium Plus”. The airline was the last of the Big Three US carriers to introduce a dedicated premium economy product, launching the cabin in 2019. Today, Premium Plus is available on most of United’s widebody aircraft, although there are some exceptions.

According to ch-aviation, United currently operates 37 Boeing 767-300ERs, 16 767-400ERs, 55 777-200ERs, 22 777-300ERs, 12 787-8s, 64 787-9s, and 21 787-10s. Of its 55 777-200ERs, 51 feature Premium Plus. The exceptions are the airline’s high-density Boeing 777 fleet, comprising 19 777-200s and four 777-200ERs, which lack a dedicated premium economy cabin.

As for the seats themselves, United uses the Collins Aerospace MiQ model, similar to American Airlines. These offer about 38 inches (97 cm) of pitch and measure between 18.5 and 19 inches (47–48 cm) wide. Passengers also receive an upgraded onboard dining service. Premium Plus meals are specially prepared and served on ceramic plates alongside metal cutlery, rather than the disposable packaging and utensils generally used in economy.

Delta Air Lines markets its premium economy cabin as “Delta Premium Select.” It first introduced the product in 2017 aboard its Airbus A350-900 on a flight from Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) to Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT), becoming the second major US carrier to offer a dedicated premium economy cabin. Since then, the SkyTeam member has gradually expanded Premium Select across its international network, including on some of its older aircraft, such as the Boeing 767-400ER.

In terms of seating, Delta’s product is quite similar to its rivals’, although it features the carrier’s distinctive diamond stitching pattern. Premium Select seats generally offer 38 inches (96.5 cm) of pitch and a width of approximately 18.5 to 19 inches (47–48 cm), depending on the aircraft. Passengers also benefit from adjustable leg rests and footrests, greater recline, larger entertainment screens, and memory foam cushions for additional comfort.

Beyond the seats, the Atlanta-based airline has built a reputation for its onboard service, and Premium Select offers several improvements over standard economy. Passengers receive complimentary beer, wine, and spirits as well as soft drinks and hot beverages. The dining service also varies depending on the route, although meals are generally served on reusable tableware rather than the disposable packaging commonly found in economy.

Overall, all three airlines offer a fairly similar premium economy experience. Unlike business class, carriers have fewer opportunities to differentiate their products, particularly when the seats are identical or closely comparable. However, all three are targeting the same group of travelers: those looking for a noticeable improvement over standard economy without paying business class fares.

Although US airlines were relatively late to introduce dedicated premium economy cabins, the product has become an increasingly important part of their business. For airlines, the appeal is also financial. Premium economy can generate around 33% more revenue per square foot of cabin space than standard economy. It can also generate approximately 6% more revenue per square foot than business class, partly because the seats take up less space and the cost of providing the onboard service is generally lower.

This helps explain why the three carriers continue to invest in their premium economy products. American Airlines is expanding the cabin across its fleet, including on its newer 787-9 Dreamliners and Airbus A321XLRs. Delta Air Lines is also placing greater emphasis on premium seating. In the second quarter of 2026, the airline’s premium ticket revenue exceeded Main Cabin ticket revenue for the first time. Looking ahead, its upcoming A350-1000 aircraft are expected to feature more than 100 premium seats, including nearly 50 in Premium Select alone.

We are also seeing a similar trend elsewhere, as airlines increasingly add premium economy cabins to their aircraft. For instance, Emirates is rapidly expanding its premium economy offering across its fleet, while Air France has doubled the number of premium economy seats on some of its retrofitted 777-300ERs. Similarly, Cathay Pacific has increased the cabin’s capacity from 34 to 48 seats on its updated 777s, representing a 41% increase.

Other airlines such as Turkish Airlines are also preparing to enter the market. The airline is planning to introduce dedicated premium economy cabins from 2028. This comes as passenger preferences are changing, especially at the higher end of the market. Looking at the wider industry, traditional first class has become increasingly rare now because airlines have shifted their focus towards business class and premium economy. In the US, American is the last of the Big Three to retain a dedicated international first class product through its Flagship First cabin, although it is now phasing it out.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Those who are willing to spend more on business class continue to do so, but premium economy has created another option for travelers who previously had to choose between economy and business. According to Going’s 2026 State of Travel and Flight Deals Report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among surveyed travelers, increasing from 16% to 20% year-on-year.

#6144. Bilt Is Changing Its Credit Card Rewards—Experts Agree: Lock In This Strategy To Earn Points Faster

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Bilt is changing how its credit cards earn rewards, and cardholders who want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spending need to make a choice. New applicants must apply, be approved and accept their offer by December 31. I’ve already opted to keep the benefit—it’s a big reason my Bilt Palladium gets most of my spending.

Frequent Miler‘s latest ‘Ask Us Anything’ was a strong endorsement of Bilt. Their three Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) cardholders plan to renew, and even the group’s Bilt skeptic plans to apply. They all want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash.

If you don’t have a Bilt card, I’d get one now. You need to apply, get approved and accept the card offer by December 31, 2026 to preserve the choice of earning 4% Bilt Cash. Existing cardmembers also need to actively choose to keep it before their first card anniversary in 2027. Doing nothing means moving into the new rewards structure.

Nick Reyes calls renewing Palladium “pretty much a no-brainer.” It’s his “daily driver,” the card he uses most often. He’s happy earning two or three Bilt Points per dollar because they’re “very valuable,” with “plenty of great transfer partners” and continued good transfer bonuses. With a points accelerator active, he’ll often use it even for spending that another card would bonus. He’s approaching Platinum status (thanks to his card spend), but says the card’s earning makes sense even before transfer bonuses and status benefits.

Tim Steinke says he expects all three Palladium holders—Greg Davis-Kean, Nick and himself—to renew and retain the current rewards structure. Stephen plans to get the card before the old earning option closes, despite having no intended use for Bilt housing payments. He calls the points “absolutely fantastic.”

That’s also how I use the Bilt Palladium Card: it gets the majority of my spending. I pay my mortgage through Bilt, but the card would be valuable to me even without that.

I’ve written that Palladium looks complicated, but it’s the best everyday rewards card.

I consider these the most valuable points. You can redeem them at 1.25 cents apiece through Bilt’s travel portal, but I usually want to transfer them. The transfer partner lineup gives me access to:

Most transfers are 1:1. Accor is 3:2, I Prefer is 1:2, and Amtrak is 2:1. Bilt also runs large Rent Day transfer bonuses, often with better offers for higher elite tiers. I’ve used bonuses for transfers to Japan Airlines, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic and Air France KLM. Earning points quickly and then transferring with a bonus is why I want so much of my spending here.

Bilt is changing the earning choice in 2027. Today, cardmembers can choose:

Most cardmembers already choose the second option. Palladium is still a great card that way. But for most people putting significant spending on the card, especially when they’re generating more Bilt Cash than their housing payments would consume, I think the 4% option is better. Once you’ve reached the highest housing multiplier, spending more doesn’t increase that multiplier. With Flexible Bilt Cash, more spending keeps producing more Bilt Cash to use.

There are exceptions. I’ve explained how the housing option can produce an effective 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. At the 25% spending threshold, $1,000 of everyday spending and $4,000 of eligible housing payments earn 2,000 points from the purchases and 2,000 from housing. That’s 4,000 points against $1,000 of everyday spending. The relationship between your spending and housing payments determines which choice works best.

For me, the accelerators alone are a reason to preserve Bilt Cash earning. Spend $200 in Bilt Cash to activate one and you earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in eligible spending. Palladium’s 2X becomes 3X. That $5,000 also generates another $200 Bilt Cash, which can fund the next accelerator. Each eligible cardholder can activate five per calendar year.

My wife and I have both maxed out our accelerators this year: 3 points per dollar on $50,000 of combined spending. We’ve earned points on housing payments as well.

She has an authorized user card on my Palladium account. It costs $95 annually and comes with her own Priority Pass membership. She doesn’t receive a second set of my annual hotel and Bilt Cash credits, but she can earn rewards in her own Bilt account (or I can switch it to mine).

I’ve laid out how my wife and I use this. I directed the points and Bilt Cash from her spending into her account instead of mine. She earns her own status, funds her own accelerators, and can take advantage of transfer bonuses separately. When an offer bonuses transfers of up to 100,000 Bilt Points per member, two accounts give us room to bonus 200,000 points, with each person’s bonus determined by their own status.

An authorized user’s spending doesn’t automatically get the primary cardholder’s active accelerator. They need to activate their own, using their own Bilt Cash. Bilt also gives the primary cardholder separate card numbers and controls over authorized user spending, including transaction and monthly limits. You can add an authorized user starting at age 13. But for my wife and me, the separate rewards accounts are the reason this has been so useful.

And I’ve gotten far more out of Bilt Cash than just faster points earning. I’ve redeemed it for:

These are benefits I’ve actually used. For my everyday spending, Palladium earns the points I want faster than any other card, and the benefits have been incredible.

The new structure still allows Palladium and Obsidian cardmembers to use accelerators. Palladium’s $400 annual hotel credit and $200 annual Bilt Cash become a $600 annual Bilt Cash deposit at the card anniversary. That can fund three accelerators. Members can also earn Bilt Cash from other activity, including $50 for each 25,000 qualifying points. But they won’t replenish it at 4% of everyday spending.

Keeping the existing structure also preserves my separate $200 hotel credits, which I can stack with Bilt Cash hotel redemptions. The Bilt Cash hotel redemption allowance moves from monthly to twice yearly starting January 1 even for those keeping 4% earning, but I can still get the two $300 discounts this way.

Plus, Bilt Cash now expires at the end of the month 12 months after it’s earned. Cash earned in February 2026 lasts through February 28, 2027. The old rule would have wiped out everything over $100 at year-end. Having more time to use what I earn makes the 4% option better for me.

If you don’t have a card, I’d apply now and complete approval and acceptance before December 31. My choice is Bilt Palladium. The ability to preserve 4% Bilt Cash also applies to the Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) and no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (See rates and fees).

And if you already have a card, don’t assume your current selection of Flexible Bilt Cash protects you from the change. You need to proactively choose to keep it. I’ve already done this:

The new rewards model is selected by default. Swipe right.

You have until your first card anniversary in 2027 to make that election. Preserve it now and you can still move to the new structure later. Once that switch takes effect, you can’t move back. That’s why getting a Bilt Palladium Card makes so much sense – keeping the earning option. They’ll pry the 4% Bilt Cash earning option from my cold, dead hands, as they say.

#6143. Delta SkyMiles Gold Card Review: Solid Perks For Occasional Delta Flyers

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card is the mid-range personal credit card in the American Express and Delta co-brand card portfolio, which includes seven cards, covering a variety of annual fee levels, across both personal and business products.

This post is my in-depth review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Amex Card. The card has a reasonable annual fee and is ideal for someone looking for basic benefits that come in handy when flying Delta. However, if you’re a Medallion elite flyer on Delta, another card might be a better option (more on that below).

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card review, here’s a quick look at the card’s main selling points and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Delta Gold Amex welcome bonus and ongoing fees, since these are some of the most important features to consider when opening a new card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex is currently offering new cardholders the following bonus: You may be eligible for as high as 80,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $2,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $880.

This is a solid welcome bonus, though the card recently offered a higher one that included a statement credit along with bonus miles. Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they’d rather wait for a better offer, or apply with this offer so they can take advantage of the perks ASAP.

The welcome offer on the Delta Gold Amex card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past.

You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal versions of the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more) or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the Delta Gold Amex first. That’s because if you do, you’d potentially still be eligible for the Delta Platinum Amex and Delta Reserve Amex. Meanwhile if you apply for one of those cards first, you’d no longer be eligible for the “lesser” card.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score you need to get approved for the Delta Gold Amex. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been denied, as it’s only one of many factors that determines card eligibility.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees). This is a great opportunity to try the card before you have to “buy” it. The card also has a reasonable annual fee on an ongoing basis, so it’s easy to recoup that fee by taking advantage of the card perks.

You can also add authorized users to the Delta Gold Amex at no extra cost.

If you are going to put spending on the card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees) with the Delta Gold Amex, so you can use the card abroad without paying those high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. Unfortunately the Delta Gold Amex isn’t much to get excited about on that front, but let’s still go over the details.

When it comes to the return on spending, the Delta Gold Card offers:

While it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling. There are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays it’s common to see airlines offer elite status qualification through credit card spending. Delta SkyMiles elite status is based on the concept of Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs), and it’s possible to earn elite status with credit card spending.

The catch is that the Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn any MQDs, so if you want to qualify for status, you’ll have to pick up the Delta Platinum Card or Delta Reserve Card. More on that later.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

As I’ll cover below, having the Delta Gold Amex also gives you access to the TakeOff 15 discount on award tickets, and that can also help you stretch your SkyMiles for travel on Delta.

The real reason you’ll want to keep the Delta Gold Card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which are great for the casual Delta flyer. Truthfully, this is the value proposition of many airline credit cards — it’s largely about the welcome bonus and the perks, so let’s take a closer look at those details for the Delta Gold Amex.

Perhaps one of the biggest incentives to actually spend money on the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is the ability to earn a flight credit. Specifically, if you spend $10,000 on the card in a calendar year, you can receive a $200 Delta eCredit to use toward future travel, which will be deposited right in your SkyMiles account. The credit expires one year after it’s issued.

Getting a $200 Delta eCredit in addition to any miles could be a good incentive to spend $10,000 on the card per year. The credit alone is the equivalent of a 2% return on spending, assuming you consider it to be worth face value.

Just for having the Delta Gold Card you receive up to $100 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $100 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $100, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex, you get a first checked bag free. You can also receive a second checked bag free on eligible domestic Delta flights.

This benefit is limited to the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for your flight with your Delta Amex, though you do need to have your SkyMiles number in the reservation.

With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up. A first checked bag on domestic flights costs $45, and a second costs $55, so even just checking one bag on two roundtrip flights could effectively cancel out the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Gold Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary card member’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation. This benefit is valid for the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation.

If you have the Delta Gold Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible inflight purchases of food and beverages. The statement credit will post within 8-12 weeks of an eligible purchase.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for 1.0 cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the Delta TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta flights booked through delta.com or the Fly Delta app. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card also comes with a rideshare credit. The way it works is that you get up to $10 back as a statement credits each month when you use the card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

You need to enroll in this benefit in order to get the money back, and it doesn’t kick in until after your first card renewal. So while it’s a useful perk if you already pay for rideshares at least once a month, it doesn’t really make or break the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in having as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. Note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card isn’t a card I’d be using for my everyday spending, since there are many more rewarding cards for that. However:

In other words, for someone who flies Delta occasionally, I think this card could make sense, and the benefits can more than offset the annual fee.

Meanwhile if you’re a more frequent Delta flyer, there could be value to having one of the more premium credit cards, which allow you to spend your way to elite status, and earn Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs).

If the Delta Gold Card sounds interesting to you, but you want a business card instead, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card. Learn more about applying for Amex business cards.

The Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (learn more) has a $0 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following benefits:

Beyond that, though, there are limited perks. If you’d get value out of a first checked bag free or priority boarding, then you’re much better off getting one of Delta’s cards with an annual fee. I can’t really see much upside to getting the Delta Blue Card, over the other options in the market.

The Delta Platinum Amex (learn more) has a higher annual fee of $350 (Rates & Fees) and offers more perks than the Delta Gold:

If you want to earn MQDs toward elite status and enjoy more Delta benefits, like an annual companion certificate, the Delta Platinum Amex is the better option between these two cards.

The Delta Reserve Card (learn more) is the most premium option among personal Delta Amex cards, with the highest annual fee: $650 (Rates & Fees)

It also has the most benefits, so it could be worth it if you frequently fly Delta and want the best perks like lounge access:

Those aren’t even all the Delta Reserve card benefits. It also lets you earn MQDs on spending and gets you upgrade priority over other Delta SkyMiles members with your same Medallion tier, product, and fare experience purchased. The annual fee is high, but it’s absolutely worth a look if you want as many Delta perks as possible.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers:

The (see rates and fees) has a strong reputation — and for good reason. With high earning rates, benefits that easily outweigh its $95 annual fee and access to Chase's transfer partners, it's easy to see why this card is a great fit for both beginners and die-hard points and miles enthusiasts alike.

This card received a refresh in June. While one change might've disappointed Hyatt fans, many cardholders came out ahead thanks to the added perks and bonus categories.

That said, no card is a perfect fit for everyone. If you're looking for lounge access, elite status or high earning rates on general travel purchases, another card may be a better option. The Sapphire Preferred works best in the hands of flexible travelers who want an easy card to maximize. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐½

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you're a prospective cardholder, you'll want to take note of these perks in particular when trying to decide if this card is worth it:

Related: Chase Sapphire Preferred statement credits: What they are and how to use them

The 's hotel credit can cover the card's $95 annual fee on its own if you use the full $100 on a stay you would have booked anyway.

Compare the Chase Travel rate with the price of booking directly before you pay. (The first $100 in eligible Chase Travel hotel purchases each account anniversary year does not earn points.)

Maximizing this credit will, on its own, put you $5 in the green against the Sapphire Preferred's annual fee.

When former TPG credit cards writer Augusta Stone used this credit, she effectively paid just $35 for a night away at the Atlanta Marriott Alpharetta.

The card also reimburses one Global Entry, TSA PreCheck or Nexus application fee, up to $120 (every four years). Charge the eligible fee to the card to receive the statement credit. If you already have a membership, you can use the credit to pay an eligible application fee for someone else. I recommend Global Entry if you travel internationally because it includes TSA PreCheck benefits.

It's worth noting that the Sapphire Preferred is one of the few cards with a sub-$100 annual fee to offer this benefit.

Primary cardholders can also get at least 12 months of complimentary Apple TV (by activating the offer through Chase by Dec. 31). Apple TV costs either $14.99 per month or $119 for the annual plan, so either way, you're saving a lot of money with this perk. Be sure to activate it soon, since you only have until the end of 2026.

With the , you'll earn Ultimate Rewards points at the following rates:

*Excludes Target, Walmart and wholesale clubs

TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens calls out the vacation homes category as a big plus for her. She's booked over 60 Airbnbs, so there's plenty of opportunity for her to earn lots of bonus points with this category.

I live in Portland, Oregon, a city with a strong mass transit system (by U.S. standards). That means I often swipe my Sapphire Preferred for transit tickets, so I'm glad that this card's general travel rewards category is broadly defined.

My main criticism of the Sapphire Preferred's earning categories is that its grocery category is restricted to online orders only. Walmart, Target and wholesale stores are also excluded from this category, which is a major downside for me as a frequent Walmart shopper. Still, this is a relatively minor critique given that the card's overall earning structure is very strong for a $95 annual fee.

You can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for a variety of options, including statement credits, gift cards, Amazon.com purchases and travel booked through Chase Travel.

The includes access to Chase's Points Boost feature, which means you can redeem your points for up to 1.75 cents per point (depending on the redemption). While Points Boost can offer solid value in the right circumstances, I generally prefer transferring my points to Chase's airline and hotel partners, where I can often get significantly more value.

Speaking of transferring points, Chase offers 14 transfer partners, including World of Hyatt, United MileagePlus, Air Canada Aeroplan and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

Personally, I transfer most of my Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt. Last year, I transferred 87,500 Ultimate Rewards points to Hyatt to book 10 nights at different hotels across Germany, easily saving me hundreds of dollars. (Note that the number of points you'd need to replicate this strategy would be higher by default with the updated 4:3 transfer ratio.)

Despite the unfavorable transfer ratio, Hyatt is still a compelling transfer partner thanks to its fixed award chart pricing. And with a deep roster of airline and hotel partners, Chase still offers plenty of opportunities for valuable redemptions with other partners.

For example, TPG's managing editor for credit cards, Giselle Gomez, transferred 22,000 Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue for a one-way flight between Miami International Airport (MIA) and Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG). Thanks to a 20% transfer bonus, she was able to save 3,000 points. This ticket would've cost $1,504 without points, so after accounting for $139 in taxes and fees, she received a phenomenal over 6 cents per point in value.

To wrap up, here is a summary of the value you can get from your Chase Ultimate Rewards points with this card:

**According to TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Related: How much are Chase Ultimate Rewards points worth?

The is one of the best travel rewards cards for its annual fee, but it isn't the right fit for everyone.

Getting the most from the Sapphire Preferred means tracking bonus categories, statement credits and partner perks. If you prefer a card that earns the same rate on every purchase, this setup may feel like more work than it's worth.

This card provides the most value to people who travel regularly and redeem their rewards for travel. While Ultimate Rewards points can be redeemed for cash back, higher value comes from booking travel through the Chase Travel portal or transferring points to airline and hotel partners. If you don't expect to use either strategy, the Sapphire Preferred may be harder to justify.

The Sapphire Preferred is undoubtedly one of the strongest mid-tier cards, but as with any other card, it's important to make sure it fits your lifestyle and travel needs.

The 's equally well-known older sibling is the (see rates and fees). This card charges a substantially higher $795 annual fee, but comes with a much wider array of perks, including:

Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt at a better 1:1 ratio, compared with 4:3 on the Sapphire Preferred. If you regularly book Hyatt award stays, factor in the value of those extra points alongside the Reserve's other benefits when weighing its $795 annual fee.

To learn more, check out our showdown between the Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Preferred.

According to TPG's valuations, that welcome offer is worth $1,538.

Keep in mind that you must be under 5/24 to be approved for the Sapphire Preferred. If you currently hold the Sapphire Preferred, previously held it or earned a welcome bonus on it in the past, you more than likely will not be eligible to earn another welcome bonus.

The card makes the most sense if you can use the Chase Travel hotel credit and redeem points for trips you would otherwise pay for. If Hyatt is your main transfer partner, factor the 4:3 ratio into the cost of your awards before deciding.

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

#6133. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.
